breakdown_rules.rule: Scale one everyday act (adding incomes) from a person to a family to a country, then prove the equality with a one-product economy in which every number is small and visible.
Follow the idea's life story: who claimed it, what the claim means on the graph, who challenged it and why, and what new term the challenge produced.
Each piece answers the next natural learner question: where did it come from, what does the word mean, who decides, what difference does it make, is it a different rulebook, what kinds exist.
Start from the goal and ask 'what does this depend on?' one link at a time until a lever is reached; name the control of that lever as the new term.
Take one dense definition sentence, cut it into its phrases, and turn each phrase into one step of a worked calculation; then ask what the result does, why it was chosen, and why it failed.
Build the normal cause chain and freeze it as a direction table; then teach the new term as the one row that breaks the table, and explain that row with a second cause chain on the same diagram.
Teach the new pair through a known pair (CPI/WPI), then build the first index as a worked table and the second as one change to that table.
One reason per piece, each told as a cause chain from 'economy grows' to 'market rises', followed by one piece for the exception.
Follow one bond through its life (issue, promise, risk, resale, return, market) and stop wherever the learner would ask a question; each question becomes the next concept.
Teach the abstract word pair with the smallest possible example, switch to a second example that brings in the real deduction, and only then write the formula and its boundary case.

Teach in two depth layers: first what the tool does to ordinary people and the economy (layman layer), then how it works inside (exam layer), and teach each opposite (reverse repo) as the mirror of the first.
Each stretch of the price-index curve with a different slope is one term; then each term gets a verdict, and the one bad term gets its own cause chain and its own cure.
Hold one quantity fixed (one laptop a year) and let only price move, so every new term is the name for what that one change does to GDP.
One quarter-to-quarter step of the curve is one teachable piece; a new term is introduced only when a longer run of steps forms a new pattern.
Keep one small market fixed and change one node at a time (demand, supply, cost); each change that moves the price is one teachable cause, named after it is seen.
Go from the whole (general price level) to the parts (items in the basket), and name the new term at the point where the parts disagree with the whole.
Each piece is the bank's answer to the problem left by the previous piece, and each answer is followed by its limit, which creates the next problem.

Every new piece is one branch hung on the same investor-to-India picture: first by route (stake or factory, above or below 10%), then by investor type, then by year of rule change, and the exception to the last rule closes the video.

Break a system statement into its named parts (fixed to gold, pegged to dollar), teach each part with one moving picture and a small number, then run one concrete transaction through the whole system and change one number to show the lever.

Each piece answers the next question an index maker must settle, in the order they settle it: what to compare (basket), against when (base year), at which point of the chain (wholesale), which goods and how heavy (groups and weights), how to price one item (quotes to elementary index), how to combine items (weighted sum), and how to read the result (base 100, monthly, point-to-point).
Cut the history at each law or committee, and give every cut the problem that caused it and the change it made, all placed on one running timeline.
Follow the foreign currency: first why it moves, then where it is kept, then how every movement is recorded and added up, and finally what the total does to the reserve.

Cut history into problems and the institution each problem produced, derive the core concept from the first chain of problems before any date, then hang every later event on one growing timeline as the response to a crisis.
Strip the data to one row (January) and add one reference idea at a time until the effect appears in the numbers.
Each system is one piece told as problem -> rule -> goal -> test -> failure or success, with the failure of one system becoming the reason for the next.
Overview then details: first show the whole problem and its fix in one panel, then return to each piece (institution, each risk) one at a time, ticking it on a sidebar map.
Follow one government bond through its life (issue, kind, return, resale), and introduce each term only at the step of that life where it is needed.
Cut the topic along the investor's worry: one piece for the risk, one for the protection that removes it, one for what the protection costs.

First the players and the two rules of the game, then one piece per instrument, each answering the same three questions on the same picture: who issues it, to whom (security down, cash up), and its limits (amount, tenure, exceptions).

Start from who owns and who is served, prove the benefit with one worked money example, then build the structure bottom-up and add each regulator only when a need calls for it, ending in a summary grid that poses the next problem.

Each piece answers a question the index maker meets in building it, in order: what is bought (six groups), over what window to ask (reference period), for whom (segments, then rural/urban/combined), how heavy each group is (weights), and how to turn prices into one number (price relative, geometric mean, weighted sum).

Cut by ratio and by rule change: for each reserve say where the money sits, whether it earns and why it exists, then its legal band and each dated change with the law or committee that caused it; the policy effect comes last from today's numbers.
One step of reading the real source per piece (who, which report, which date, which row, what it means), then widen the time frame.
Start from one problem picture (who is not reached), give the official reasons, then teach each new institution as features or limits that answer those reasons, each limit with its 'why'.
Each candidate definition is tested on a small made-up country; when its numbers break the definition, the fix becomes the next teachable piece.
Cut the history at each law, and before each law ask the question the law answers (why private? why nationalise? where to start? how to reach the regions?).
One piece per exam statement: match it to the single lecture node that decides it, judge it true or false from that node, and carry the verdict to the answer options by elimination.

teaching_orders.order: A textbook draws the circular flow and lists the product, income and expenditure methods as definitions. Here the video ties off the last lesson (variants, base year), then asks a puzzle: if GDP is a sum of products, why does it give national income? The answer starts from the learner's own pocket (my income, then my family's, then the whole country), states the surprising three-way equality as a claim, and then proves it with an imaginary economy that makes one laptop. Claim before proof, small before big.

A textbook draws the short-run curve and the vertical long-run curve and defines NAIRU. Here the topic is told as the life of an idea: a provocative quote, the man and his data, his claim read on the curve, its fame, the challenge by two later economists, their reason, and the new term their challenge left behind. The learner first believes the trade-off, then watches it break on the same curve, and the natural rate is defined only when the dot needs a place to stop.

Textbooks usually give the types first and the definitions after. Here the order is history, the law that created the split, what 'schedule' means, the criteria, why the status matters (benefits), a common misconception, and only then the types tree. 'Why it matters' comes before the long list, so the list lands on a reason.

A textbook defines monetary policy first and then lists its objectives, its committee and its instruments. Here the video starts at the goal (growth) and walks backwards, asking each time 'what does this depend on?': growth needs price stability, stability depends on inflation, inflation on demand, demand on purchasing power, purchasing power on money, and only liquid money counts. Monetary policy then arrives as the answer (control the lever you found), followed by who decides (MPC) and the tools, which are left for the next video. The term comes last, as a conclusion.

A textbook would define NEER as a formula and list India's regimes by date. The video starts from where the last one ended (the 1971 collapse), puts the 1971-92 period on a timeline and cuts it in two, then takes the dense official sentence for 1975-92 and breaks it phrase by phrase ('basket', 'major trading partners', 'weighted average'), working each phrase with assumed numbers in a table until the NEER pops out. Only after the learner has computed it does the video ask what NEER moving up or down means, then asks 'what was the purpose?' and lets the learner infer it, and finally shows the mistake and the 1991 devaluation. It ends by re-zooming the whole timeline and explaining why the next two videos come in the order floating, then LERMS.

A textbook defines stagflation first and then lists its causes. Here the video first builds the normal rule (GDP up, unemployment down, inflation up, and the reverse) as a long cause chain, fixes it in a three-column direction table, ties it to the Phillips curve already taught, and only then introduces stagflation as a 'twist in the story' that breaks one cell of the table. The 'how can this be?' question is answered with a different cause chain (oil prices) on the same economy diagram, so the exception is understood against the rule.

A textbook would define NEER and REER and give their formulas. This video starts from everyday prices moving unequally, recalls how CPI and WPI answer 'is inflation rising?', and mirrors that question for the currency, so NEER and REER arrive as the expected answer. NEER is then built as a worked table, REER as one extra column on the same table, and a comparison with a memory rule closes it.

A textbook would list the factors that link markets and the economy. This video first states the link as an observation (the market is a barometer), asks 'why?', answers with four numbered cause chains hung from the same anchor diagram, and then adds the exception (short-term disconnect) with its causes. Claim, then why, then exceptions: the order of an argument.

A textbook defines a bond, lists its features (face value, coupon, maturity, rating, yield) and then explains primary and secondary markets. Here a company needing money for a project starts it; the bond is introduced as a promise and its two obligations are drawn as a money loop. Then the learner is scared on purpose (the company runs away with your money) before credit ratings are introduced as the protection. Resale is told as one bond passed along a chain of investors, and yield and the two markets are both read off that same chain, so the later concepts are new readings of one picture rather than new topics.

A textbook states NDP = GDP - depreciation and then defines depreciation. Here the video first contrasts the words gross and net in plain language, then works a tiny farm example where the 'deduction' is seed, then switches to a factory where the deduction is machine wear (depreciation), takes a side road into why firms like depreciation (tax), comes back to compute gross and net for the factory, and only then writes the NDP and NNP formulas, closing with a boundary rule (business phone vs personal phone). The formula is the conclusion of two worked examples, not the start.

A textbook defines repo as a repurchase agreement first, then reverse repo, then LAF as the framework, then limits. Here the video starts from the learner's own loan, climbs one level (banks borrow from RBI), and shows the effect on ordinary borrowing before any mechanism. It then teaches the policy effect (rates down, liquidity up) and names LAF, and says outright that this is enough 'as a layman'. Only then, 'for UPSC', it opens the mechanism: collateral, the sale-and-buy-back that gives the name, the discount in numbers, why overnight borrowing happens, variants and limits. Reverse repo is taught last as the mirror image of repo. The order is effect first, mechanism second, in two depth layers.

A textbook lists four definitions side by side. Here the video first recalls where prices are measured (two baskets on one supply chain), then lets the slope of one price-index curve name three terms (rising, rising slower, falling), checks them on real CPI data, and only then judges each as good or bad. Reflation is held back to the very end: the deflation harm chain is built first, so the cure is felt as needed before it gets its name (problem before fix).

A textbook defines nominal GDP (current prices) and real GDP (constant prices), then gives the deflator formula. Here the video first settles last video's question, re-states that factor cost is the better production indicator, and then breaks that belief: with one laptop a year and 10% inflation, GDP still rises every year. Only after the learner sees GDP rise with no extra output are the names given (inflated, then nominal; remove the inflation, then real). The method follows the same laptop back along a year line to a base year, the deflator is the tool that does it, and the four-way tree comes last as a summary.

A textbook lists the definitions one by one. Here one hypothetical curve is walked from left to right in time, so the terms come in the order an economy would live them: growth, faster growth, slower growth, contraction, recession, depression. Each later term is built out of the earlier ones (recession = contractions in a row; depression = a long recession), so the time order is also the prerequisite order. The spoken agenda lists the terms in a different order from the one taught.

A textbook defines demand-pull and cost-push with a formula-like sentence each and a diagram of shifting curves. The video names the two causes and the two schools up front, then teaches everything with one tiny market (one bread shop, two packets, two buyers at 50 rupees) and changes one thing at a time: more buyers, then fewer packets, then a costlier factory behind the shop. Each time the term is given only after the price has visibly moved. The second school is taught last, as a frame that sits under the first school's whole tree and claims one cause (more money in people's hands) under both branches.

A textbook would define skewflation in one line. This video first rebuilds inflation and deflation as moves in a basket's overall price, then opens the basket to show items moving unequally, and only then names skewflation as the case where a few items race ahead while the average looks normal. A real case and the term's origin come last. Whole first, then the parts, then the term where the parts disagree with the whole.

A textbook defines MSF in one line (banks borrow overnight from RBI against SLR securities at a rate above repo) and then lists its limits. Here MSF is the last answer in a chain of problems: reserves are kept, the rest is lent, what cannot be lent sits idle and is parked in G-secs, then a new customer arrives and the money is stuck (objection voiced), repo solves it up to a limit, the worked numbers hit that limit at 20 crore, demand doubles to 40 crore, and only then MSF enters. The rate rule comes after the mechanism, with a reason (penalty for poor liquidity), and real history comes last.

A textbook would define FDI and FPI side by side, then list investor classes and regulations. The video keeps one picture (foreign investors -> India) and grows it as a tree: it splits into FDI and FPI, finishes the FDI branch completely (two routes, one real case each, then why a company would bother), recaps that branch, and only then opens FPI, which it tells as a chain of years (1994 FII, 2011 QFI, 2014 merger, RFPI rename, risk categories). The rule (must register with SEBI) is stated last and immediately followed by its exception (P-notes), which becomes the cliff-hanger for the next video.

A textbook would start with Bretton Woods as a dated institution and list fixed vs floating regimes. The video starts from the learner's last lesson (devaluation helps exports), asks the questions that lesson left open, and goes into history to answer them. It then splits the system into two named sub-questions (what 'fixed to gold' means, what 'pegging' means), answers each with a moving picture, names the regime only after showing all currencies tied together, and makes the regime concrete with a running character buying an imported car. Devaluation is then shown as the central bank's lever inside that same money path, and the collapse closes the loop on the gold link stated at the start.

A textbook opens with 'WPI measures the average change in wholesale prices', then lists the base year, the basket, the weights and the formula. Here inflation gets one line, then a household scene (this month's ration cost 5000; an elder says it used to cost 1000) builds the idea of comparing one basket at two times, and only then are 'basket' and 'base year' named, as labels for parts of the story. The supply chain (factory, wholesaler, shop, buyer) places WPI between PPI and CPI and gives a reason to care (a producer-side rise warns of consumer inflation) before the video narrows to WPI. The calculation is taught on one object, a chair, from 11 price quotes to its index, and that number is then joined by one line to its row in the weight table, so the big formula is built from a case the learner has already followed. How to read the result (100 in the base year, monthly, point-to-point) and who publishes it come last.

A textbook lists the nationalisation Acts with dates, then the aims, and treats 1991 reforms in a separate chapter. Here one timeline runs through the whole video and each step is told as problem, then law, then institution, then result: SBI's reach is still small, private banks ignore farms and small industry, so the 1969 and 1980 Acts follow; the whole period is then folded into one era band and its gains are listed. The next problem (crisis) turns the band red, leads to a committee, its reforms, and their place inside LPG, and the video ends by splitting the timeline at 1991 into before and after, so nationalisation and privatisation are seen as two eras of one story. A cliff-hanger on banking reforms leads to the next video.

A textbook opens with the definition of BoP and its format. Here the video starts from the need: buying from abroad costs foreign currency and selling earns it, so a country must keep a reserve, and the reserve rises or falls. Only after a long list of dealings is the umbrella name given (BoP statement). Then the format is built top-down as a tree, and the arithmetic is built bottom-up (each head nets to plus or minus, heads add to account balances, accounts add to BoP). The end returns to the reserve from the first minute, so the whole format is framed as 'what decides whether the vault fills or empties', and the crisis is the vault running dry.

A textbook lists dates in order: 1683 Madras Bank, 1770 Bank of Hindustan, 1806-1843 presidency banks, 1860 Act, 1921 Imperial Bank, 1935 RBI. Here the video opens on the present (banks you see around you), then spends four minutes deriving what a bank is through the East India Company's business problems: obstacles, a middleman, a cash shortage, loans at interest, limited funds, public deposits at a lower rate, and only then 'these agency houses are now working like banks'. Dates start only after the concept is clear. The earlier banks (1683, 1770) come as a flashback correction ('it is not that there were no banks before 1806') by extending the timeline to the left. After that each new institution follows a crisis (war panic, then merger; depression, then RBI), and the video ends on a puzzle (a privately owned RBI) that the next video answers.

A textbook defines base effect first and then gives an example. Here the term is named only after the numbers have already shown the effect: base year = 100, cut to one month, index vs inflation reference years, the formula, equal rises giving a falling %, and only then the name. The puzzle comes before the label.

A textbook lists PLR, BPLR, base rate and MCLR with definitions and dates. The video starts with the problem as a lived scene (a customer haggling a loan rate down like vegetables at a cart), names the system only after the scene, then tells each later system as a repair of the previous one's failure: each rule is introduced with its goal, tested (a 2010 report, staged as a second role-play between RBI and the banks), shown failing, and replaced. The cause of failure (banks competing for customers) was already planted in the opening scene by the rival bank's lower offer.

A textbook starts with BIS and the Basel Committee, lists Basel I-III with dates, and then defines capital adequacy. Here the video starts with the danger: running a bank is risky, a failed bank cannot repay depositors, and one failure spreads to all banks, to industry and to the whole world. The Basel norms come in as the protection (keep money aside, like spare cash in an inner pocket on a bus), then the institutions behind them, and only then each risk is taken apart, credit risk as a full story. The format is overview first, details after, with a sidebar map that lights the current risk; the capital ratios are named but left for later.

A textbook starts with G-secs and their types (T-bills, dated securities), then pricing, then yield as a formula. Here the video first maps the whole capital market as a tree and walks a road-map down to the government security market, so the learner always knows where the topic sits. Inside, it follows the life of one bond: issued by the government through RBI, first at a discount (zero-coupon), then without a discount, where the learner's objection 'why buy it then?' brings in the coupon. Numbers compare the two kinds side by side. Then the same bond leaves the primary market and changes hands in the secondary market; yield is named only after the first resale is computed, and the inverse rule is drawn last from the story's own numbers.

A textbook would define CDS as a credit derivative, then list the parties and the premium. This video starts from a feeling (losing sleep after lending money), recalls why corporate bonds are risky, and only then brings the CDS in as the fix, and last its price: problem, then solution, then the cost of the solution. Each step answers the worry the step before raised.

A textbook usually gives a table of instruments with issuer, tenure and minimum size. Here the game comes before the pieces: the market is hands passing money from surplus to scarce, the tree narrows to the organised market (the unorganised branch is ticked off as done), then who may play, then the two rules (no paper, no money; deal only within your level), then what a security is (by an underworld analogy), and only then the instruments. Instruments are grouped by issuer (government, banks, firms through banks, banks among themselves, banks with RBI, top companies, savers), and each is drawn on the same template (issuer, security down, cash up, a name bar, a limits callout), so the learner compares instead of memorising. Where three parties or a promise to buy back are involved (commercial bill, repo), a story or a what-if comes first and the term arrives as its name.

A textbook usually defines cooperative banks, gives their history and then the structure (short-term rural tiers and urban banks) and regulators in a list. Here the definition is a scene (a local community starts a bank that serves the same community), objectives follow, and the commercial bank is placed beside it as a mirror (owners vs users). Before any structure, a full worked village example shows in rupees why a community would do this (better deposit and loan rates, reserves kept, still a small profit shared as dividend). Then the structure is built bottom-up from empty tier slots (tier 1 first, then district, then state), registration comes as the learner's own question ('which office do I go to?'), and the regulators enter one by one as each need appears (society needs a registrar; bank needs a licence; health needs inspection), ending in a grid whose dual and triple control sets up the next video.

A textbook opens with 'CPI measures the change in retail prices of a basket bought by households', gives the series (CPI-IW, AL, RL, then CPI rural, urban, combined) with base years, then weights and method. Here the order follows how the index is built from the consumer upward: first where consumer price sits on the chain, then everything a consumer buys sorted into six groups, then the practical question of how many days of spending to ask about for each group (the term 'reference period' and MMRP come after the reasoning), then the problem that consumers differ, which motivates segmentation, the four segment CPIs and their uses in pay. History enters as a critique (segment CPIs are partial), which explains why rural, urban and combined CPIs exist; weights and the calculation come last, carried by one egg from price quotes to CPI-Urban. Each later part is justified by a problem left by the earlier one.

A textbook usually defines CRR and SLR together, states their purpose as monetary tools and then gives the legal ranges. Here the video builds one picture from the bank's NDTL: a first arrow to a vault held by RBI (CRR), a second arrow to a safe kept by the bank (SLR), so where the money sits and whether it earns is clear before any law. The purpose of SLR comes as a bank-run what-if. Then it walks the law (ranges, 2007 amendment) twice, once per ratio and once as an era table, then the history curves with the 1991 committee as the cause of each turn, then the wider SLR securities (closing a question it left open at 112 s). The policy use (raise to cool inflation, cut to support growth) comes almost last, after today's numbers are worked into the 77.5% lendable share.

A textbook goes definition, components, figures, history. This video assumes the definition (previous video) and follows how you would look the figure up: who publishes it (RBI, weekly), open the latest report, read its as-on date, read the total, make the total meaningful (record high, months of imports), see its parts, then zoom out to 75 years and the world rank. It teaches a habit of reading the official source, not only facts.

A textbook would define small finance banks and payments banks with their eligibility, capital and permitted activities. The video starts with the gap (a 140-crore crowd of which banks reach only a shaded part), states the national goal, lists RBI's reasons why ordinary banks cannot close the gap, and only then introduces differentiated banks as the answer. Small banks are taught as three features each answering a reason (target the poor in a fixed area, cut cost with technology, also serve city slums). Payments banks are taught as a story (wallet apps already reached the unbanked, so RBI licensed them), then their limits are explained with reasons and a loophole RBI anticipated. Examples and the naming rule come last.

A textbook gives the two definitions side by side and a table of differences. Here the video offers the common definition (rising GDP), breaks it with a made-up country whose population outruns GDP, repairs it (per capita income), breaks it again with a second made-up fact (poverty rises, literacy falls), asks 'why?', answers by following where the money was spent, and only then names development. The history (trickle-down and its failure) comes after the concept, as the story of how economists learned the same lesson; a cliff-hanger on measuring development closes it.

A textbook lists RBI's founding, its nationalisation, then SBI and its subsidiaries as dated facts. Here history is told as a series of puzzles and answers on one running timeline: a strange fact first (the RBI was privately owned), 'why did the British do this to us?', two reasons; then the Act's promise, independence and the 1948 law that keeps it. The SBI story starts from the needs of a new country (development, industry, funds, private banks refusing priority sectors and villages), weighs two options (build new banks or take over existing ones), asks 'where to start?', and answers with the biggest bank. Each step is cause, then law, then institution change; the video opens on the previous video's last canvas and ends on the canvas the next video opens with.

A textbook teaches each topic fully and puts questions at the end of the chapter. Here the order is the exam paper's: question first, concept second. Each statement is read, then the exact lecture node that decides it is fetched and replayed, then the verdict goes back onto the statement and is pushed through the options by elimination. Inside a question the statements are checked in the order the lecture tells them, not the paper's (Q2: the founding history decides statement III first; Q4: the borrowing figure gives the fiscal deficit before revenue and primary deficits). The Q4 primary-deficit formula is reused at once in Q5, so the learner meets the same rule twice in two minutes. Q6 finds the answer by eliminating on one false number (45% vs 41%), then confirms with one true statement. This works as retrieval practice for revision: the learner sees what an exam asks about a concept and which one node of the lesson answers it.

talmel_summaries.summary: The first minute is text: typed variant lines the voice never reads, then about 36 s of base-year talk over a nearly still frame. From 70 s the picture carries the argument together with the voice: one person grows into a family and then a row of people inside the map, the laptop gets factor arrows and paid/sold arrows, and the same 10,000 lands on each sigma term as it is spoken. The picture leads by 1-3 s when the equation and the laptop enter, which works. Weak: income sources are not labelled, and the family's parts are shown but never spoken.

The best fit is the dot on the curve: it climbs while bars on both axes grow and shrink, then slides back to the natural rate as the wage chain is written, and later sits still while push arrows and piling hatch lines show inflation speeding up. Here the picture truly shows the process. The biography leans on a real photo, a journal cover and notes that copy the speech; the wage chain is text only. Once the voice gives the wrong direction ('unemployment comes back down') while the picture moves the right way, and the recap is spoken over promo and the end screen.

In the first half the picture shows steps: a law-book drops on 1934, the bank forks, a Loan note rides the RBI arrow, often a few seconds before the words. In the second half the picture becomes a list: 10 of 24 changes are tree labels typed exactly on the spoken name, which matches perfectly but adds nothing to the words. One note adds a fact (the 1949 Act) that the voice never says, and the spoken caveat about payments banks is not marked on the tree.

Picture and voice build the backwards chain together: each 'depends on' is placed to the left as it is spoken, and one blue band then traces the whole path from liquid money to growth. The CONTROL arms move from inflation to liquid money to show where RBI acts, and the chain collapses into the MONETARY POLICY badge just as the term is said: the picture shows how the term is made. The house-and-plane story is drawn with icons and a red cross. Weak: definition boxes land 6-20 s before the voice defines, the two kinds of tools are grey text boxes, and ten tool names appear without speech under a promo overlay.

The calculation half fits well: the basket of mixed notes tied by a rope to the rupee turns 'pegged to a basket' into a picture, and the table fills row by row as each weight and rate is spoken, ending in a lit answer column and the single number 0.048. The cause half drifts to text: the NEER-up/down boxes, the purpose answer, and the misalignment chain are statements stacked on screen, often several seconds before the voice. A home-base composition (strip, basket, rope, rupee) is returned to three times, which keeps the learner oriented.

Most of the picture is words: text chains and a direction table whose cells fill as the voice says each direction, so the picture often repeats the speech. It works when structure carries the meaning: the red stagflation row under two green normal rows shows the broken pattern at a glance, the STAG|FLATION split shows the word's parts, and the oil shock is worked through the same economy flow. Weak spots: a long sentence box lands 10-20 s before the voice reaches it, and the 1970s date is only on screen while the voice says 'suppose'.

In the NEER part the picture walks the calculation step by step on the same words (weight, rate, multiply, add), but the actual numbers are on screen only and never read. The analogy panel (inflation question above the currency question) is the strongest fit of speech and picture. REER gets a column that is never filled, and the closing rule is a '<' sign plus text, so the picture stops showing meaning exactly where the new idea arrives.

The anchor band (economy, chevrons, rising market lens) is the one place where the picture carries the meaning; after it, the reasons are text nodes that mostly restate the speech, some 2-4 s early. Picture and voice disagree once (voice: demand falls; node: demand rises), and the stories (boasting, FOMO, panic selling, war) get no picture, so the most memorable spoken parts are the least shown.

Mostly together, and the picture often shows the step: the money loop (investor's money up, face value and coupon back on dotted lines), the spotlight on the issuer for the rating agency, one bond passed down a chain with the coupon arrow following the holder, a column of return under each holder, and a panel sliding along the same chain for primary and secondary market. A persistent sidebar mini-map of the topic tree moves its box at each signpost, which keeps the learner oriented. Weak: letter-grade rating ladders and the selling steps are text the voice never reads, and the yield formula has no numbers.

The example objects (farmer, sack, machine line, phone) usually appear 1-5 s before the words, and computed values fill waiting chips as they are spoken. The picture shows the step best in the gross-to-net arc labelled '- depreciation', the machine's falling value curve, the expense card set beside the profit card leading to NO TAX, and the YES/NO paths for the two phones. Weak: the profit card arrives long after the profit is spoken, the government card and rule box copy the speech, and the wheat values are not visible on the chips in the sampled frames.

checks_learned.check: Items listed on screen should be spoken, or marked as reference only; here four variants are typed but never read.
Every amount in a spoken running sum needs its source label next to it (YouTube, rent, job were spoken but not written).
Every number shown in an addition should be spoken, or the voice should say the parts are on screen (the family addends were silent).
A spoken change over time (base year 2004 to 2012) should appear as a change on screen.
Flag more than about 20 s of speech over an unchanged frame (27-63 s here).
When a claim is stated before its proof, the claim's picture (the equation) must stay visible and each proved value must land on its own term (worked well here; enforce it).

Direction words in the speech (badhna / ghatna / neeche / upar) must match the direction of the animated quantity at that moment; here the voice said unemployment comes down while the dot moved to higher unemployment.
The same date range must not be given two ways in one script (data 1861-1957 vs a title ending 1965) unless the difference is explained.
A person's name must be said the same way every time (Phelps later said as 'Phillips').
A term should be explained within about 15 s of being named; here the natural rate was named at 189 s and explained only at 216 s.
No end-card or promo overlay may start while teaching speech is still running, and the recap must sit on the final teaching picture.
When an acronym is expanded in speech (NAIRU), the expansion should be written beside it at the same time.
Trivia read aloud over a still frame (thesis title) should be cut or turned into a short note card.
A spoken misconception needs a 'wrong idea, crossed out, right idea' beat on screen, not just a note.
Screen text must not add a fact the voice never mentions (here the Banking Regulation Act, 1949) unless the voice pauses to point at it.

A classification list of more than about 4 leaves should not be typed leaf by leaf for close to a minute; group it, give one example per leaf, and show what is missing on the other side (no public sector bank or RRB among unscheduled banks).
A spoken caveat about a leaf ('no payments bank is unscheduled today') must mark that leaf on the picture.
After each classification the script should answer 'what difference does it make?'; this video does it with an explicit learner question, and it should be a rule.
A definition box should not land more than about 3 s before the voice reaches that definition (here 20 s early for price stability and 6-10 s for liquid money).
Names shown only on screen (the tool lists) must be spoken or marked 'next video', and must never be covered by a promo overlay.
When a term is derived from a chain, the compression of the chain into the term's badge should land within about 1 s of the spoken term (worked well here; enforce it).
In a backwards chain, each new cause must be placed upstream of the last one with its arrow pointing to the effect.
Every actor in a story picture should be labelled by role (here the cash-holding rival buyer and the plane seller are not clearly told apart).
A list of everyday examples spoken one after another should be sorted into its groups on screen as each is said, not shown as two finished bullet lists.
Counts said must match counts shown (the voice says 6 partner countries, the table shows 5).
A dense definition shown as a note should be followed by a phrase-by-phrase unpack, each phrase highlighted as it is explained (E05 does the unpack; the highlight is missing).
A worked calculation should show every row being computed in step with the voice; rows done 'the same way' may fill together, but the total must be spoken (E05 does this).
A cause shown only on screen (convertibility suspended, at 9.6 s) must be spoken at least once.
Long-standing condition boxes (NEER up / down) should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice starts them.
A promo overlay must never cover a recap view.
A question to the learner ('what was the purpose?') should leave a short pause before the answer appears on screen.
A sentence box should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches its content (here a wages box led by 10-20 s).
If the voice frames an example as hypothetical ('maan lijiye'), the screen must not add a real date the voice never says; either both say it or neither.
Every cause chain the narration finishes ('yaani inflation rise karega') must end in a drawn node for that last step.
An exception must be drawn in the same table or diagram as the rule it breaks (the red row under the green rows worked; enforce it).
After a question to the viewer, the answer must return to the same cell that held the '?' and replace it.
A term written on screen must be spelled the same in every video of the series (PHILIPS vs Phillips).
When a worked table gains a column for a second method, the column must be filled and the new total shown (here the REAL column stays empty and no REER number appears).
Numbers in a worked example must be read aloud or pointed at at least once (walk the first row: 30% of 0.012 gives 0.0036).
A formula shown on screen must be read once, or walked with one substitution.
A 'remember this' rule (REER above NEER means higher inflation) needs its reason in one spoken line or a picture; a bare '<' sign fails.
A new concept that mirrors an old one should be shown side by side with it in the same structure; this video's CPI/WPI to NEER/REER panel is the model.
A direction word spoken in a cause chain must match the node on screen (the voice said demand 'decreases', the node says increased); flag any increase / decrease mismatch between script and picture.
Every spoken link in a cause chain should get a node; here the price rise, the reinvestment and 'market rises' are spoken but not drawn in reason 1.
A story or role-play voice (boasting, fear of missing out, panic selling) should get a small scene; a bullet alone fails.
A list of causes shown as bullets for more than about 30 s needs one mini picture per cause.
A fixed anchor diagram at the top with each reason hanging under it works; each reason's chain should end with an arrow back onto the anchor.
An inverse rule in a formula (yield = fixed interest / price) must come with a small worked number example at two prices; this video has none.
Reference tables shown on screen (agency letter-grade ladders) must be cut to what the voice uses (top grade vs low grade) or read aloud.
A risk scenario (company runs away) should be followed by its safeguard within the same scene (done here; enforce).
A persistent topic mini-map should move its highlight on the same beat as the spoken signpost (done here; enforce).
Procedure steps (trading account, documents, sell order) must be drawn as a step flow, not a paragraph.
Promo overlays must not cover canvas text while narration is still teaching.
Claims about the present state of a real market ('very small') should carry a date.
Numbers inside one example must agree with each other (a 30% yearly rate does not take 20 years to reach zero); a code check can test rate x years against the stated life.
Every value the voice computes (net 90, net 70 lakh) must appear on its waiting chip at that moment.
A card for a spoken quantity must appear within about 2 s of the first time it is spoken (the profit card came about 25 s late).
Year labels on screen must match the spoken year (the voice puts the 30 lakh drop in 2022, the table shows 70 lakh against 2023).
Flag an aside longer than about 40 s that the target terms do not need; claims about real companies need a source or must be dropped.
The opening and closing checklists must tick exactly the items the voice says are covered.
Narration and on-screen text must agree on who does what in a deal (voice: RBI promises to repurchase; screen: the bank does); a script-scene consistency check should compare actor roles.
A year spoken and a year written must match (LTRO: transcript 2000, screen 2020); re-transcribe BIE's own narration and compare numbers and years with the scene text.
No stretch longer than about 20 s of narration should run over a still canvas; the 80-s overnight repo story needs its own scene (report deadline, short cash, overnight loan, repayment).
A worked example that promises a calculation (4% for one day) must finish it with the actual figure on screen.
Opposite mechanisms should reuse the same diagram mirrored, with only the direction and one word changed (worked here for reverse repo).
A policy effect taught by a state swap (decreased to increased on the same diagram) is a reusable pattern for two-direction cause and effect.
Labels that rename a rate ('rate of discount') must be checked against the book; flag terms the source does not use.
Reasons that sound like rule-dodging (borrow overnight to show a clean CRR/SLR report) must be checked and worded neutrally.
The closing recap should restate the links between terms, not only list their names.
A good/bad verdict about a term must put a visible mark on that term's own picture; flag more than about 20 s of speech over an unchanged frame.
When a spoken example uses numbers (7% to 4%), those numbers should be labelled on the picture they describe.
A stretch of real data labelled with a term must match the shape rule taught for it (disinflation = still rising, only slower); a flat stretch should not carry that label without saying why.
A policy cure (reflation) should be drawn as tools acting on the same curve, not as a caption sentence read aloud.
The colour given to each term must stay the same across the made-up chart and the real chart (worked well here; enforce it).
Branches of a tree should be drawn in the order the narration names them (unemployment was named before NPAs).
The closing recap should be spoken over the finished pictures, not the end card.
A worked formula result must agree with the running example it reuses (12,100 / 10 = 1,210 while the peel-back story landed on 10,000); a numeric consistency check should catch it.
When an index such as a deflator is used, its scale (base = 100) must be stated with the number.
Every derived cell in a table should be reached by an arrow from its source cell (done here; enforce).
When a term is transformed into another (nominal into real), strike the old word and write the new one at the moment the voice says it (done here; enforce).
Reasons given only as text cards for more than about 20 s (the 2015 switch) should be flagged for a picture.
BIE must not show real organisation emblems (UN flag) or invent viewer names for shout-outs.
Keep the varying quantity to one: holding output at 1 while price changes isolated the idea cleanly; a check can require one variable changing per numeric example.
A term defined as a pattern of steps (recession = two contractions in a row) must be drawn as one band spanning exactly those steps on the same chart.
The agenda should list terms in the order they will be taught.
The recap must be spoken over the finished chart, not over the end card.
The defining words must match the slope on screen: a GDP fall must not be called a 'declining growth rate' when the same video teaches slower growth as a separate idea.
Axis and unit setup before the first term should stay under about 20 s or state why it matters.
A spoken number change (6% to 7-8%) about a chart piece should get a label on that piece.
Every number on screen must be spoken (60 and 55 appear only on screen).
A number should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches it (65 leads by about 9 s).
When the voice says something is unchanged (demand, supply in cost-push), the screen should mark it unchanged; E15 does this only for the bottleneck case.
Comparing causes should reuse one scene and mark only the node that changed (E15 does this; enforce it).
A stretch of more than about 60 s with only text boxes (the Monetarist view) should be flagged for a picture.
A transcript where one token repeats many times is a failed transcript: re-run with language detection before any timing check (E15's narration was English, forced Hindi produced loops).
If a case is named as a subtype of two things (bottleneck from a supply drop, yet 'still demand-pull'), the lesson must say plainly how both hold.

A real case with two numbers to compare (above 20% vs below 11%) needs a picture of the comparison (for example two bars); flag a canvas that stays unchanged for more than about 30 s while a case is told.
When the voice says some items fall, at least one item on screen must show a down arrow.
No promo overlay may cover the canvas while a teaching sentence is being spoken.
Term nodes that pop in about 0.5-1.5 s before the spoken term work well; flag nodes more than 3 s early, or after the word.
A definition box that repeats the voice word for word should be replaced by the visual it describes or cut.
Every percentage written on screen (4.5%, 18%, 77.5%) must be spoken, or labelled as 'current value' with its date.
Two different values for the same quantity in one video (gap 'back to 1%', then 'today 0.25%') must be caught by a consistency check and resolved in the script.
When a worked number example runs, each derived number must land on the arrow or actor it belongs to (done here; enforce).
A rule given as a written formula (repo + penalty = MSF) should be followed by the same rule in numbers (6.5 + 0.25 = 6.75) on the same screen.
Imported real-data charts must be redrawn from data, and any line the voice does not name (reverse repo) removed or named.
A new mechanism laid over an old one gets its own colour, and the old channel fades when the new rule is explained (worked here).
BIE's own narration audio should be re-transcribed and matched to the script; a stretch over 10 s with no recognised words flags a dropped or garbled line (this video's transcript lost about 50 s).
A threshold in a definition (10% stake) should be drawn as a quantity against a marked line, not only written; the same for a stated stake (77%).
A cause_effect list (benefits of FDI) shown as text bullets should be flagged; each cause needs a picture of the step (goods crossing a customs gate vs made inside).
Every acronym must be unpacked at first mention (E18 does this for all six; enforce it).
A long sub-branch (more than about 90 s) should end with a recap on the anchor picture before the next branch (E18 does this at 130 s; enforce it).
The second side of a contrast (QFI 'fewer regulations') should not appear on screen before the voice has finished the first side.
When the voice names two names for one thing (RFPI officially, FPI in the news), the screen should show both, linked.
A term named in the closing (offshore derivative instrument) must get at least a one-line yaani unpack, even if the detail is deferred.
Real brand logos and real takeover names should be replaced by generic companies in BIE's own lessons.
Questions promised in the agenda (depreciation vs devaluation, who does it) must be answered in the lesson or explicitly deferred; flag open promises at the end.
Every number on screen must be spoken (±1% is on screen; the voice says 'some percent').
Every effect named on screen must be spoken (balance of payment crisis is only on screen).
The agent on screen must match the agent in the voice (screen: government devalued; voice: central bank devalues).
After a rule change (devaluation), re-run the same running example with the new number (E19 does this with the car; enforce it).
A definition note should not appear more than about 3 s before its term (the hard-peg note leads by about 6 s).
No caricatures of real people or brand founders; BIE uses its own recurring characters.
A humour beat must not replace the bridge question's teaching; the question should still be spoken and pictured.
A question put to the viewer (arithmetic vs geometric mean) must be answered later in the same video, or the script fails.
Every number shown on screen must be spoken or labelled as reference: here 20 Rs, the chair's 193.77 and the 2022-23 monthly values were shown but never said.

When a story sets numbers (1000 then, 5000 now) and a formula comes later (current / base x 100), the formula must be applied to the story's numbers once (index 500 vs rise 400%); here that link was missed.
A data table on screen shows only the rows the narration names; a 22-row weight table held for 44 s with one value spoken should be collapsed or stepped through.
Named formulas and proper nouns (Laspeyres, Jevons, DPIIT) need a pronunciation entry for BIE's voice and subtitles taken from the script, since recognition garbled them here.
A running example started on one item (the chair) must be carried into the aggregate step on screen (done here with one line from I1 to W1); enforce for every worked calculation.
Time-bound remarks ('we are in December 2022', months not yet available) must carry a date stamp or be removed.
Claims flagged for fact review against the source book: WPI for macro vs CPI for micro policy, and 'point-to-point' explained as comparison with the same month of the base year.
Idle decorative animation (a waving flag) must stop while teaching changes happen; 4 of 24 change points here were only the flag.
Absolute claims ('100% nationalised', 'all industries') must be flagged for a fact check before narration; the card notes this one is not accurate.
When a count carries the point (14 banks, 85% of business, 7 associates), draw that many items or a filling share, not only a text note.
A text-only screen held for more than about 20 s with no drawn actor should be flagged (private-bank paragraph, before/after boxes).
In a history video every law or committee should have a spoken cause before it and a spoken effect after it (this video mostly does; enforce).
History videos should end by clearing to the bare timeline as a recap (done here; enforce).
Same-name items (Committee I and II) must have the reason for the numbering spoken (done here; enforce).
Constant decorative motion (the spinning globe) must stop during teaching beats; it hid two minutes of changes from the change detector and competes with the step being taught.
A list of dealings that each move money in or out should be drawn as flows into or out of the reserve, with direction, not as a bullet list.
A 'yaad rakhiye' rule that splits one thing two ways (principal vs interest) must show both halves on screen; only the interest half was drawn.
A topic built on plus/minus balances needs at least one small worked number example; this video has none.
Every short form shown on screen (BoT, NFIA, CAS, CAD) must be expanded by the voice at first use (done here; enforce).
A definition side note (BoP crisis) should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches the term, and promo banners must not cover the canvas while the final definition is spoken.
More than about 8 new terms per minute in a classification tree should trigger a split into two scenes or a recap.

Every date, 'first' and 'only' in a history script must be checked against the book source before narration (here: Madras and Bombay years look swapped; 'world's only privately owned central bank' and 'Britain's central bank was government-owned' are doubtful for 1935; agency houses described as Indian lalas and seths).
The opening hook must not contradict the body (the hook says PNB and Allahabad Bank began under the British; the body calls them private joint-stock banks, PNB with Lala Lajpat Rai).
A spoken cause chain with actors and actions (panic, withdrawals, banks failing) must get a picture in the scene plan, not only a note; flag 'chain with no picture'.
A merger must be shown as the merging things joining (three buildings sliding into one), never only as a text note.
A timeline object must not appear more than about 3 s before the narration reaches it (three buildings appeared about 11 s early).
When a story derives a concept ('agency houses are now working like banks'), the scene plan should relabel the same actor at that conclusion line (worked here).
On-screen notes must pass a spelling and grammar check ('Presidency Houses' for presidency banks; 'owned entirely was private shareholders').
Emotive national framing in history ('why did the British do this to us') must be flagged for neutral wording.
A history video with more than about 15 dates should end with a spoken and drawn timeline recap.
Present-day bank logos used as examples should be replaced by generic buildings with name labels.
Numbers that carry the punchline (here 10%, 9%, 8.3%) must be spoken or pointed at by the voice, not only appear on screen.
The term being defined must be named while its diagram is still on screen; no promo or end card may start before the term and its conclusion line are finished.
When a formula is read aloud, highlight each table cell as it is used and substitute real numbers at least once.
Flag any table that stays unchanged for more than about 20 s while the narration moves on.
In a cause-effect concept the cause must be said in one plain line (the same rise on a bigger base gives a smaller %), not left for the viewer to work out.

In a role-play opening, the term is named only after the scene ends, and the later explanation of failure must point back to a moment of the scene (here the rival-bank offer becomes the competition reason).
When a number in a running example is revised, the old value stays visible and struck, so the history of the change can be read.
Every item of an on-screen list must be spoken (three of the four base-rate inputs are never said).
A text answer must not appear more than about 3 s before the voice gives it (the 'because banks were competing' line leads by about 6 s).
Key evidence numbers (77% of lending below the floor) must be drawn as a quantity against the floor line, not only written.
Goals planted as on-screen chips must be resolved on the same chips (cross on failure, tick on success); E25 does this well.
Statements about who decides (RBI fixed BPLR vs BPLR settled with banks) must stay consistent within one lesson; flag contradictions between narration lines.
When two successive systems are compared, reuse one scene and change only the parts that differ (tag, ring, arrow direction).
A spoken analogy must get a picture in the scene plan; here the strongest idea (inner-pocket cash on a bus) has none.
Content promised 'in this video' (CAR, CRAR, RWA, tier capital) must be delivered or explicitly moved to the next video before the end.
Spoken years and numbers must match on-screen text (Basel 1: transcript 1998, screen 1988); a check should compare them and flag for audio review.
Abbreviation-to-full-name lines with no idea drawn (CAR, CRAR, RWA) should be flagged as names without meaning.
A consequence chain (failure, contagion, credit crunch, downturn) must be drawn as a chain, not as bullets.
'Prices fluctuate' needs a moving price line; a list of asset names does not show market risk.
A sidebar chapter map that lights the current part worked; enforce it for overview-then-details videos.
Every input of a spoken result must be spoken or shown at the same moment: a yield of 10% needs its price (5,000) said, not only placed on a later graph.
Every computed percentage in the script must match its arithmetic and one rounding rule (500/9,000 = 5.56%, shown as 5.5%).
A story the narrator tells about a name (golden edges on British bonds) must get a picture in the scene plan; flag 'story with no picture'.
Real bank and company names and logos as characters must be replaced by generic actors (Bank A, Company B).
A teaser line ('important concept in the next 2 minutes') must name the concept, and the scene that pays it off must follow within the stated time.
When two terms differ on one yes/no property (sold at a discount?), the scene plan should use a yes/no fork (worked well here).
Definitions that narrow or redefine a standard term (G-sec only for non-discounted bonds; yield as interest in the secondary market) must be checked against the book source and flagged.
On-screen definition paragraphs over about 25 words should be split into labelled steps or replaced by the picture of the process.
A taxonomy of more than about 8 nodes before the first example should be cut to the path the lesson takes; the rest shown only as a road map.
A promo overlay must never cover a recap screen.
When the narration names a transfer between parties (risk moves from A to B), the scene must move one object from A to B; a text label alone fails.
A conditional rule (if X defaults, B pays A) needs the trigger event and the payout drawn as steps (a default mark on the bond, a money arrow from B to A), not only a paragraph.
On-screen rule text must not appear more than about 3 s before the voice starts saying it.
Idle character loops count as decoration: flag a scene where more than a third of the visual changes carry no meaning.
A pain named in the hook must be visibly resolved when the concept solves it (awake to asleep), before the end card.
A 'regular' or 'periodic' payment must be animated as at least two repeated pulses.
A worked example must obey the limits of the instrument it illustrates: the T-bill example used a 2-year security while T-bills run 364 days at most.
Every step the narration gives a mechanism must be drawn: the repo buy-back (securities returning, cash plus interest going back) and term money were spoken but never shown.
An exception that contradicts a definition given earlier (CDs by AIFIs for 1-3 years still called money market instruments, though money market means up to 364 days) must be reconciled in the script.
Sibling concepts reuse one picture template (here: issuer, security down, cash up, name bar, limits callout for T-bill, CD and CP); BIE's scene plan should enforce one template per family.
No scene may sit unchanged for more than about 30 s while new terms or limits are spoken (participants strip about 140 s, CD about 60 s).
Real brand logos (a named bank) and real state emblems must be replaced with generic icons.
Speech-gap detection must use word start times: a 12 s loss inside one segment (763.7-776.0 s) was invisible to segment-end checks.
A one-line 'seen from the other side it is X' (repo vs reverse repo) needs its own picture and a check against the source book, since the term has a narrower policy meaning in India.
A running money example must balance: parts sum to the whole (75 + 18 + 4 + 3 = 100 lakh) and the tally equals its rows (7.5 + 1.08 - 3 - 5 = 0.58 lakh); worked here, enforce in code.
Number checks that compare transcript and screen must understand Hindi 'each' doubling ('teen-teen lakh' heard as '33 lakh'), so a false alarm is not raised and a real mismatch is not missed.
A worked example must say whether members' money is a deposit (earns interest) or share capital (earns dividend); here the same 1 crore is treated as both.
Leftover cash and yearly expenses are different things; 'the remaining 3 lakh is spent on expenses' should be flagged as a stock-flow mix-up.
Structural claims (UCBs under DCCBs, UCBs serving PCS) must be checked against the book source.
Regulatory facts must carry an 'as of' date (the 2020 Banking Regulation amendment changed RBI's powers over co-op banks); 'NABARD regulates' should read 'supervises/inspects' if the book says so.
Real bank logos used as characters must be replaced by generic bank marks.
A list with a moving highlight should not hold one canvas for over about 30 s; each item gets a small scene or the list is cut.
One colour per entity type kept through the whole video (worked here: yellow PCS, orange UCB, dark green DCCB, light green state bank); enforce as a scene check.
A table of results should reveal row by row as each row is spoken, not all at once 5-20 s early.
A worked example must be named in the narration: here the egg, its index 150.40 and its weight 0.36 appear only on screen; every number the calculation lands on must be spoken.

A question to the viewer must get a real answer: the WPI video's open question (why the geometric mean) is answered here only as 'international practice'; BIE should give the reason (an outlier quote pulls an arithmetic mean more).

When two videos teach the same method (WPI and CPI calculation), BIE should reuse the same scene template and say so ('the same steps as WPI'), and keep the formula names and pronunciations identical.

Claims flagged for fact review against the source book: which bureau compiles CPI-UNME, the example jobs for industrial workers (IT sector), the foreign-company DA use of CPI-UNME, and the start year of CPI rural/urban/combined.
No real-person photo, brand pack or stray mouse cursor may appear in a BIE scene; replace with generic icons and clean renders.
A table of many numbers (18 weights) must be read as a comparison: show only the cells the narration discusses, or turn the columns into bars.
A rule stated as text tags (MMRP, 'partial index') needs its own picture: for MMRP, three windows of different length on a calendar.

A sentence repeated by an editing slip (the calculation start said twice) should be caught by a script check for near-duplicate consecutive lines; about 31 s of garbled or missing speech should be flagged by word-start gap and repetition checks.
Legal sources named in a script must be checked against the book (here both ratios are tagged 'RBI Act 1949'; CRR is usually under the RBI Act 1934 and SLR under the Banking Regulation Act 1949).
Every 'current value' (CRR 4.5%, SLR 18%) must carry its date and be compared with the run date; stale values are flagged.
Eligibility lists (which assets count as SLR securities) must be verified against the source before narration; this list looks wrong.
A recap table should not be rebuilt cell by cell right after the same rules were taught (about 100 s here); reveal it whole as a summary.
Lists of more than about 4 items should become a sort-into-groups scene or icons, not lines of text written one by one.
A policy effect (what changing the ratio does) must get its own scene: the dial moves and the lendable arrow shrinks or grows.
An open-loop question ('for now take the answer as no') must be closed later in the same script; pair them in a check (done here at 415 s).
Framing check: 'RBI wants to raise inflation' should read 'RBI accepts some inflation to support growth'.
Re-transcribe BIE's narration; a gap of more than 10 s without words (508-522 s here) flags a dropped line.
Spoken time words ('today', 'aaj ki rate') must agree with the date on screen; flag a 'today' claim shown with an older dated note.
Screenshots of real sources with unreadable text should be redrawn as BIE's own simple table holding only the rows the narration uses.
Every big number should carry a unit and a scale anchor (months of imports, times since a year); this video does it and it should be a rule.
Content on screen at the start (the four-part sum) must be spoken or marked as recall within about 5 s.
Voice timing must be word level and complete; a recognition gap over about 5 s blocks talmel checks and should fail the voice stage.
Counts said must match lists shown (10 small banks said; the table shows more rows).
Dates on screen must match the narration (wallets 'from 2006' in voice, 'before 2013' on screen).
No real person photos or quotes as decoration; cite the source in text only.
Every 'not allowed' rule should be shown as a struck item or a blocked arrow (E34 does both; enforce it).
A reasons list held as text for more than about 40 s should be flagged; each reason needs its own small picture.
Elements with no stated meaning (the row of thin up-arrows) should be flagged as decoration.
Superlative claims ('first in the world') must be marked for fact-checking before reuse.
Reusing the opening problem picture for a later idea (the crowd box for wallets) should be encouraged, so the learner compares slices.
Made-up country figures must carry an on-screen 'example, not reality' note while they are shown (E35 does this; enforce it everywhere).
Every number shown on screen (138 crore) should be spoken, or dropped.
An actor the picture adds (the government as spender) must also be named by the voice.
When the voice rejects a definition, the screen must visibly strike it (the red cross on the growth title worked; enforce it).
A derived value (per capita = GDP / population) should show its division step on screen, not only the results.
Notes that repeat the narration should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches them.
A cliff-hanger close must still recap what was settled before opening the next question.
Superlative claims ('first and only fully private central bank in the world') and who-did-what claims (who bought the 92% stake) must be flagged for a fact check before narration.
When an on-screen reason differs from the spoken reason (public trust), the scene check should flag the mismatch.
History narration should keep timeline order, or mark a flashback on screen; here the 1937 move is told after 1947.
Names shown on screen but not spoken (eight associate banks) should be either read or placed on a map, not left as a list.
Idle flag animation produced 2 of 24 change points; decorative motion must pause during teaching beats.
Series continuity: open on the previous video's last canvas and end on the canvas the next one opens with (done here; worth keeping as a rule for multi-part topics).
Every law on a history timeline should have its question or cause spoken before it (done here; enforce).
Spoken option letters in an elimination must match the options crossed on screen (here 'A, C and D' was said while a, b, d were crossed): a script-vs-scene check.
Every numeric question needs its working drawn on screen (formula, then numbers, then result); Q5 showed only a tick after 30 s of still page.
Every figure given in a question that the solution does not use must be named as a distractor with the reason (the 10,000 non-debt receipts in Q5).

Generated practice: each false statement must differ from a true fact in exactly one checkable element (number, category, actor or an extreme word), and must carry a link to the lesson node that refutes it.

When the answer is reached by elimination, the narration must say which statements no longer need checking and why, and one surviving statement should be confirmed positively (Q6 did the confirmation but not the explanation).
An evidence scene must restate its fact in the narration; text that only sits on screen (the bovine definition, census numbers, vertical and horizontal) does not count as taught.
BIE must not reuse lessons as filmed screens with small text; an evidence scene is re-rendered on the canvas, with the lesson's own narration line included in the script and subtitles.

Speech recognition lost about 245 s here, mostly replayed lesson audio: when BIE builds a practice video from lesson clips, the clip lines must come from the script, not from re-recognition, and any 10 s window with no recognised words is flagged.

games.player_does: Is the entrepreneur of a one-laptop country: rents land, hires workers, borrows capital and pays each factor by dragging coins, then sets the laptop's price and sells it to a buyer.
games.process_happens: Each payment fills a factor reward (rent, wages, interest, profit) and builds the laptop's cost; when the buyer pays, three meters fill: total income, total product value, total spending.
games.win: All three meters show the same number.
games.lose: Setting a price above what was paid out leaves a gap between meters that is labelled 'this extra is also someone's income: profit'; once profit is counted the meters match again.
games.concept: income = products = expenditure

games.player_does: Matches each factor of production to its reward: land, labour, capital, entrepreneur with rent, wages, interest, profit.
games.process_happens: A correct match draws a blue arrow from the factor into the laptop and puts the reward on the income band.
games.win: All four matched and the laptop is built.
games.lose: A wrong pair (land with interest) makes that worker or owner walk off, and the laptop stays half built, with the right pair shown.
games.concept: factors of production and their rewards

games.player_does: Taps people to add their incomes: first oneself, then family members, then rows of people across the map, keeping a running sum.
games.process_happens: Each tapped person's income flies into the sum; at country scale the sum becomes the NATIONAL INCOME chip and the equation appears beside it.
games.win: Reach the country total and predict that the product and spending totals will be the same.
games.lose: Counting someone outside the border shows the person standing outside the map with a 'not inside the territory' note.
games.concept: national income as the sum of everyone's income

games.player_does: Is the central bank and turns an inflation dial each year to cut unemployment.
games.process_happens: In the short run the dot climbs the curve and the unemployment bar shrinks; after a few years wage-demand cards play (prices up, workers ask for raises, firms cannot pay all, firing) and the dot slides back to the natural rate while inflation stays high; pushing harder piles up hatch lines without moving the dot.
games.win: Keep unemployment at the natural rate with steady inflation for ten years (find NAIRU).
games.lose: Pushing unemployment below the natural rate makes the inflation meter run away while unemployment returns, which teaches the long-run critique.
games.concept: short-run trade-off vs long-run natural rate (NAIRU)

games.player_does: Orders cards to explain why the trade-off breaks: high inflation, higher living costs, demand for higher wages, firms cannot pay everyone, firing, unemployment back to the natural rate.
games.process_happens: Each correct card moves the dot one step back along the curve and writes the step in the chain box.
games.win: Dot back at the natural rate with the chain complete.
games.lose: A card out of order freezes the dot and shows which earlier step is missing.
games.concept: why the trade-off fails in the long run

games.player_does: Places idea cards on a timeline: 1950s thesis on UK data, 1958 publication, 1960s fame, early 1970s challenge, natural rate and NAIRU.
games.process_happens: Each placed card changes the curve on screen: it appears, grows famous (gets a crown), gets a 'short term' label, then the label is struck and 'long term' and NAIRU appear.
games.win: Timeline complete and the final curve matches the video's last picture.
games.lose: Putting the challenge before the publication shows a crossed-out curve with nothing to challenge yet.
games.concept: the life of the Phillips curve idea

games.player_does: Plays RBI at the list desk: bank cards show paid-up capital, reserves, liquidity and solvency; the player decides which banks go into Schedule II under the current criteria. An 'economy event' card then changes the criteria.
games.process_happens: A cash crunch follows: listed banks draw cheap repo loans (green note riding the RBI arrow), unlisted ones must borrow from the market or pay a red higher emergency rate; customer stars drift toward listed banks.
games.win: The list matches the criteria after every change and no weak bank fails in the crunch.
games.lose: Listing a weak bank makes it fail in the crunch (why the criteria exist); leaving a strong bank off makes it pay a high rate and lose customers (why the status matters).
games.concept: Schedule II criteria and the benefits of scheduled status

games.player_does: Drags bank cards (a public sector bank, an RRB, a small finance bank, a payments bank, a local area bank, a foreign bank) into a tree: scheduled or unscheduled, then commercial or co-operative.
games.process_happens: Each correct drop grows a leaf on the tree the way the video does.
games.win: Every card placed in a branch where it is allowed.
games.lose: Dropping a public sector bank or RRB on the unscheduled side bounces it back with the rule; a payments bank on the unscheduled side is accepted but tagged 'none today'.
games.concept: types of banks

games.player_does: Starts at Economic Growth and drags 'depends on' cards to the left one by one: price stability, inflation, demand, purchasing power, money, liquid money.
games.process_happens: Each correct card snaps in with its arrow pointing toward the effect; when liquid money is placed, the RBI CONTROL arms slide under it and the chain folds into the MONETARY POLICY badge.
games.win: Chain complete and the badge formed.
games.lose: A card placed with the arrow the wrong way plays the wrong claim aloud (for example 'inflation creates money') and shows the contradiction on the chain.
games.concept: root cause of inflation and what monetary policy controls

games.player_does: Holds a wallet of assets (5 crore house, FD, PF, PPF, cash, savings account) and must buy a 25 lakh plane offered for one day only; chooses which assets to use.
games.process_happens: Blocked assets show 'months' timers and a rival with cash takes the plane; liquid assets complete the purchase, the demand meter rises and the price meter ticks up.
games.win: Buy in time using only liquid money and sort every asset into blocked or liquid.
games.lose: Choosing the house or FD shows the rival flying off with the plane, with the note 'rich on paper, no purchasing power today'.
games.concept: blocked vs liquid money and why only liquid money makes demand

games.player_does: Seats six people at the MPC table: the RBI Governor in the chair, a Deputy Governor, a nominated RBI official, and three members from the government side.
games.process_happens: Each correct seat lights a member; when all six are seated, the committee gets a liquid-money tap with a dotted (indirect) and a solid (direct) handle.
games.win: Correct committee, then bring inflation into a target band by turning the right handle.
games.lose: Putting a government member in the chair shows the [Chairman] tag jumping back to the Governor.
games.concept: MPC composition and direct vs indirect tools

games.player_does: Fills the basket: sets each partner's weight from a trade-share bar (they must add to 100%) and drags in each partner's per-rupee rate.
games.process_happens: Each row computes weight x rate in the answer column; the column sums into the NEER number, which hangs from the basket tied to the rupee note.
games.win: Reach the target NEER for the given year with weights that match the trade shares.
games.lose: Weights that do not add to 100% leave the basket lopsided and the NEER cell blank; a wrong product lights that row red.
games.concept: how NEER is calculated

games.player_does: Moves a NEER slider up or down and predicts what happens to the rupee and to the trade deficit before the system plays it.
games.process_happens: NEER up: the rupee note rises against the basket, exports shrink, the deficit bar grows; NEER down: the reverse.
games.win: Predict all four links correctly for both directions.
games.lose: A wrong prediction replays the chain with the mismatched link highlighted.
games.concept: NEER, appreciation/depreciation and the trade deficit

games.player_does: Runs India's exports to the US while the rupee stays pegged to the partner basket; rival exporters (China, Indonesia) can depreciate against the dollar.
games.process_happens: When a rival depreciates, its goods get cheaper on the US shelf, India's orders fall, the reserve meter drains toward a BoP crisis; the learner can hold the peg or devalue in steps.
games.win: Keep exports and reserves alive, which needs a timely two-step devaluation.
games.lose: Holding the peg too long shows India's shelf emptying and a BoP crisis banner, as in 1991.
games.concept: why the basket peg failed and led to the 1991 devaluation

games.player_does: Places regimes on a 1944-today strip: Bretton Woods (to 1971), peg to pound (1971-75), basket/NEER peg (1975-92), LERMS (1992-93), floating (1993-).
games.process_happens: The strip colours green for fixed and blue for floating as cards land, with the 1991 devaluation marker.
games.win: Strip complete and two-coloured correctly.
games.lose: Placing floating before LERMS shows the next-lesson note: LERMS needs floating explained first, but came first in time.
games.concept: India's exchange-rate regimes over time

games.player_does: For each scenario card (boom, slump, oil shock), sets an up or down arrow under GDP, inflation and unemployment before the system plays it.
