games.process_happens: The economy flow runs the scenario: factories hire or fire, wages and prices move, and the table row fills with the real directions.
games.win: All three arrows right for every scenario.
games.lose: Using the normal rule on the oil shock (inflation down because GDP is down) turns the row red with a big '?', and the oil barrel's cost band on raw material shows why prices rose anyway.
games.concept: normal pattern vs stagflation

games.player_does: Builds the oil-shock chain by dragging cards onto the economy flow: oil price up, raw-material cost up, production cost up, prices up, demand down, growth slows, GDP down, unemployment up.
games.process_happens: Each placed card lights its node on the flow and the meter it touches moves (price meter up, GDP meter down).
games.win: The finished chain ends with both the price meter up and the GDP meter down: the STAGFLATION tag lights.
games.lose: A card in the wrong place makes a meter move the wrong way, and the narrator line explains which link was skipped.
games.concept: cost-push cause of stagflation

games.player_does: Runs a factory in a growing economy and decides wages each quarter to keep and attract workers while rivals bid for the same staff.
games.process_happens: Higher wages raise unit cost; the player chooses whether to raise shelf prices; the town's price level and unemployment meters update.
games.win: Stay staffed and profitable through the boom.
games.lose: Keeping wages low loses workers to rivals; raising them without raising prices wipes out profit, showing why boom wages end up as inflation.
games.concept: GDP growth -> low unemployment -> wage-cost inflation

games.player_does: Sets trade weights for six partner currencies (must total 100%), then sees one month's exchange-rate moves and calls whether the rupee appreciated or depreciated; in level two, switches on each country's inflation.
games.process_happens: The table multiplies and adds live and shows NEER and its change; in level two the REAL column fills, REER appears beside NEER, and the rupee coin grows or shrinks against the basket.
games.win: Correct appreciation / depreciation calls for five months, and a correct prediction of whether REER ends above or below NEER.
games.lose: Weights not adding to 100% lock the sum; calling 'appreciated' when NEER fell shows the rupee coin shrinking against the basket; ignoring inflation shows REER drifting away from NEER.
games.concept: NEER calculation, its reading, and REER

games.player_does: Matches parts of the inflation toolkit to their currency twins: basket of goods to basket of currencies, price change to exchange-rate change, consumption weight to trade weight, CPI/WPI question to NEER/REER question.
games.process_happens: Each correct pair lights up both panels side by side, as in the video's mirrored layout.
games.win: All pairs matched.
games.lose: Pairing 'basket of goods' with 'inflation adjustment' shows the mismatch: the currency basket holds currencies weighted by trade.
games.concept: need for a currency index (analogy with CPI/WPI)

games.player_does: Plays a small investor over many quarters: the economy line moves (mostly up) while event cards arrive (bad news about a company, a war abroad, an RBI rate change, neighbours boasting about gains); each turn chooses buy, hold or sell.
games.process_happens: Crowd moods (panic, fear of missing out) push the stock-market line away from the economy line for a few turns, then it drifts back to follow the economy.
games.win: End with more wealth than a 'panic seller' bot by holding through short dips that the economy line does not share.
games.lose: Selling on a one-off news dip locks in the loss, and the replay shows the market rejoining the economy line soon after.
games.concept: long-run link vs short-term disconnect; market sentiment

games.player_does: Drags cards into order between Economy and Stock Market: people earn more, spending up, demand up, prices up, sales and profits up, profits reinvested, market up.
games.process_happens: Each correct link sends a chevron along the band and lifts the market lens chart a little.
games.win: A complete chain lifts the market chart to the top.
games.lose: Placing a wrong card (for example 'demand down') breaks the flow and the lens chart dips, showing prices falling instead.
games.concept: reason 1: customer spending chain

games.player_does: Holds a bond with face value 1000 and coupon 100 a year; each round the market price moves with demand and supply, and the player decides to keep, sell or buy another.
games.process_happens: The bond moves along the chain of holders and the coupon arrow follows whoever holds it; under each holder a yield column shows 100 / price paid as a percent.
games.win: End with a yield above the coupon rate by buying below face value.
games.lose: Buying above face value shows the yield column below the coupon rate, with 'price up, yield down' lit.
games.concept: bond yield vs coupon rate (inverse to price)

games.player_does: Splits savings across bonds of several companies, each shown with a rating on the green-to-red ladder and a coupon rate (lower-rated pay more).
games.process_happens: Years pass; coupons arrive by dotted arrows; some low-rated companies 'run away' or go bankrupt and their arrows stop and the principal vanishes.
games.win: Get back all principal with steady coupons.
games.lose: Chasing the highest coupon on red-rated bonds loses principal, showing why the rating matters.
games.concept: default risk and credit rating agencies

games.player_does: Sorts deals into primary or secondary market: company sells new bonds to you, you sell to a friend on the stock exchange, a fund buys from another investor, the company issues a second batch.
games.process_happens: Each card lights the matching part of the chain (cream panel for company-to-first-investor, blue panel for investor-to-investor) and moves the sidebar box.
games.win: All deals placed correctly.
games.lose: A wrong card lights the panel on the wrong link and shows who the seller is in that deal.
games.concept: primary vs secondary market, selling on the stock exchange

games.player_does: Runs the only ketchup factory in the country for a year: sets how many bottles to make and their price, and watches the machine work.
games.process_happens: The machine's value bar drops by its depreciation as it runs; at year end the player fills the Gross Produce and Net Produce chips and the system checks them (gross = bottles x price, net = gross - depreciation).
games.win: Both chips right, and the NDP equation lights with the player's own numbers.
games.lose: Leaving depreciation out makes net equal gross; the machine's lost value flashes in red beside the chip as the missing deduction.
games.concept: net = gross - depreciation (NDP)

games.player_does: Drags items into 'counts for NDP' or 'does not count': factory machine, delivery van, phone used for business, phone used personally, family car, office laptop.
games.process_happens: Each item travels the YES path into the depreciation column or stops at a crossed NO, as in the video.
games.win: All items sorted.
games.lose: Putting the family car in 'counts' shows its NO path, with the note that only assets used to produce goods and services count.
games.concept: which depreciation counts in NDP and NNP

games.player_does: As the farmer, decides how much of the harvest to keep back as seed for next season before selling the rest.
games.process_happens: The sack splits into 'seed kept' and 'available'; the Gross Produce and Net Produce chips fill with the harvest and harvest minus seed.
games.win: Keep enough seed to repeat the harvest and read off the net produce correctly.
games.lose: Keeping no seed shows next season's empty field, which teaches why the input must be deducted to see what was truly produced.
games.concept: gross vs net produce

games.player_does: Plays RBI with two dials, repo rate and reverse repo rate, and a target (inflation high: cool lending; slowdown: boost lending). Banks decide each round whether to borrow from RBI or park surplus with it.
games.process_happens: Arrows animate: solid loans flow down at the repo %, dotted parked money flows up at the reverse repo %; each bank's liquidity bar fills or drains and its loans to people grow or shrink.
games.win: Bring lending to the target zone by moving both rates the right way.
games.lose: Cutting rates during high inflation floods banks with liquidity and the loan arrows to people multiply; the panel shows 'rates down, liquidity up'.
games.concept: cutting or raising both rates raises or lowers liquidity

games.player_does: Plays a bank short of cash for one night: drags 100 rupees of government securities to RBI and signs the agreement, then next day buys them back.
games.process_happens: RBI pays 100 minus one day's interest at the chosen repo rate; the next day the bank pays 100 and gets its securities back; the gap is shown as RBI's earning; the word 'repurchase' lights up on the agreement.
games.win: Meet the night's shortfall and correctly state who buys back what.
games.lose: Trying to keep the securities after the date shows the agreement clause and a penalty; mixing up who repurchases flips the arrows and shows the reverse repo instead.
games.concept: repurchase agreement: securities as collateral, sale and buy-back, name unpacked

games.player_does: Given a bank's NDTL (for example 2000 crore) and a cash need, chooses how much to take by repo, term repo and LTRO.
games.process_happens: Limit bars fill: 0.25% of NDTL for repo (5 crore), 0.75% for term repo (15 crore), with durations shown (overnight, 7-28 days, 1-3 years).
games.win: Cover the need within all limits with durations that match it.
games.lose: Asking past a limit is refused with the % rule shown; using overnight repo for a 2-year need shows the bank having to roll over every night.
games.concept: borrowing limits as % of NDTL with worked numbers (2000 crore)

games.player_does: Sets each year's inflation rate with a slider, year after year.
games.process_happens: The price-index curve grows; each new stretch is coloured by itself: yellow INFLATION when the rate is positive, green DISINFLATION when it is positive but lower than last year, pink DEFLATION when it goes below zero.
games.win: Draw what a mission asks, for example 'bring inflation down from 7% to 3% without deflation'.
games.lose: Pushing the rate below zero turns the stretch pink and opens the deflation chain (buyers wait, demand falls), so the learner sees that slowing inflation is not the same as falling prices.
games.concept: inflation vs disinflation vs deflation

games.player_does: Plays the government in a town where prices keep falling and shoppers say 'next month it will be cheaper'; picks policy cards: raise public spending, cut taxes, cut interest rates, or wrong cards such as raise taxes.
games.process_happens: Right cards push the price level up, shoppers start buying, profits recover, layoffs stop and the NPA meter falls; the word REFLATION lands when the curve turns up.
games.win: Stop the slide and get the price-index curve rising gently again.
games.lose: A wrong card deepens the chain one step (demand down, then profits, then jobs and loans), showing each link of why deflation hurts.
games.concept: why deflation hurts and how reflation works

games.player_does: Colours stretches of a real price-index chart with three markers.
games.process_happens: Each marked stretch gets its label and tick sticker as in the video; the slope of the stretch is shown beside the choice.
games.win: Every stretch marked correctly.
games.lose: Marking a rising-but-slower stretch as deflation shows the line still going up, with the note that prices fall only when the line goes down.
games.concept: spotting the phases on real data

games.player_does: Runs a one-product economy for five years, setting how many laptops are made and the inflation rate each year.
games.process_happens: The table fills (quantity, price, GDP); the GDP block grows with a yellow inflation stripe; a second block shows real GDP at base-year prices.
games.win: Make real GDP grow three years in a row (more laptops), not just nominal GDP.
games.lose: Raising only inflation makes nominal GDP climb while real GDP stays flat; the 'inflated GDP' tag appears and the stripe fills the block.
games.concept: nominal GDP vs real GDP

games.player_does: Reads news-style claims ('GDP up 12%, so we made 12% more goods') with the year's inflation given, and taps the error.
games.process_happens: The stripe slides out of the GDP block, showing how much of the rise was inflation and how much was real; arcs hop back to the base year.
games.win: Correctly split each rise into inflation and real growth.
games.lose: Accepting the claim shows the stripe still inside the block and the real growth much smaller than claimed.
games.concept: removing inflation back to a base year

games.player_does: Places cards (real/nominal, factor cost/market price, constant/current prices, includes taxes/excludes) onto the four-leaf GDP tree.
games.process_happens: Each leaf fills; when all four are right, India's leaf (nominal at market price) lights with the 'kyun?' tag.
games.win: All four leaves correctly built and India's choice found.
games.lose: Putting 'constant prices' under nominal flashes the inflation stripe back into the block.
games.concept: four ways of calculating GDP; India's choice

games.player_does: Drags each next quarter's GDP point up or down on the chart, quarter by quarter.
games.process_happens: The step frame lands on the new piece and labels it (growing faster, growing slower, contraction); two falling quarters in a row shade a red RECESSION band by themselves; a long red run turns into DEPRESSION.
games.win: Draw the pattern a mission asks for, for example 'slow the economy down without a contraction' or 'a recession that recovers before it becomes a depression'.
games.lose: Pulling a point below the last one when slower growth was asked shows a CONTRACTION label, so the learner feels the line between slower growth and an actual fall.
games.concept: growth vs slower growth vs contraction vs recession vs depression

games.player_does: Gets short runs of quarterly GDP numbers and sorts each run into growth, slower growth, contraction, recession or depression.
games.process_happens: Each sorted run is drawn as a curve with the frame or band the video uses.
games.win: All runs sorted correctly.
games.lose: A single falling quarter put under recession shows only one red piece, with the note that recession needs two in a row.
games.concept: recession as two contractions in a row

games.player_does: Runs the one bread shop: each day an event card hits (more buyers arrive, a packet is lost, the factory raises its price), the learner sets the day's price and then tags the cause as demand-pull, bottleneck or cost-push.
games.process_happens: Buyers with 'ready to pay' tags line up; at the learner's price the packets move to the buyers who can pay and crosses fall under the rest; the node that changed (demand, supply, cost) lights up on the supply - price - demand line.
games.win: Sell out every day without losing money and tag every cause correctly.
games.lose: Too low a price leaves a long queue and an empty shelf; too high leaves bread unsold; a wrong tag replays the day highlighting the node that really changed.
games.concept: demand-pull vs bottleneck vs cost-push

games.player_does: Sorts news cards (festival crowds rush the market, a flood ruins the wheat crop, bakery wages rise, a sudden ban on a raw material, a cash bonus for every family) into demand-pull, bottleneck (structural) and cost-push.
games.process_happens: Each card, when dropped, plays on the bread-shop scene: buyers multiply, packets vanish, or the factory's cost chip rises, and the price tag moves.
games.win: All cards placed with the matching scene change.
games.lose: Putting the flood under cost-push shows that only the shelf emptied while the factory cost stayed the same, with a nudge to look at the supply node.
games.concept: classifying causes of inflation

games.player_does: Controls how much money is in the two buyers' wallets while the factory raises its cost and the shopkeeper tries 55.
games.process_happens: With no extra money the buyers refuse 55 and bread sits unsold until the price falls back; with fuller wallets 55 sticks; adding money with no cost change also pulls the price up.
games.win: Show a price rise that lasts, and notice it lasts only when wallets grow.
games.lose: Raising cost alone shows the price spike and fall back, with the Monetarist note 'cost-push is not independent'.
games.concept: Monetarist view: inflation needs more money in people's hands

games.player_does: Watches a basket of eight goods month by month with only the overall price gauge visible; can 'open the basket' (costs a turn) to see each item's arrow; each month calls it: normal, inflation, deflation or skewflation.
games.process_happens: Item arrows grow by different amounts and the overall chip shows their weighted average; in some months two items (food) race ahead while the average stays normal.
games.win: Call skewflation in the right months and name the racing items.
games.lose: Calling skewflation when every item rises together shows that this is plain inflation; watching only the gauge and missing the racing items replays the 2009-10 case (WPI calm, food above 20%).
games.concept: skewflation vs inflation

games.player_does: Sets how much each of eight goods' price rises this year.
games.process_happens: The arrows grow to match and the overall price chip moves to their average; the tree under the basket lights inflation, deflation or neither.
games.win: Hit a target overall inflation with at least one item falling, showing items can disagree with the total.
games.lose: If two items are pushed far above the rest while the total stays on target, the screen flags skewflation instead of a pass.
games.concept: overall vs individual prices

games.player_does: Runs a bank with NDTL 2000 crore for one day. Customers arrive with loan requests (5, 10, 20, 40 crore); when spare cash runs out, the player chooses a source: repo, term repo or MSF, and drags G-secs to RBI as collateral.
games.process_happens: The G-sec moves up to RBI, a loan comes down the matching channel with its rate, and the loan goes out to the customer; limit bars fill (5 crore repo, 15 crore term repo, 20 crore MSF from the SLR safe).
games.win: Serve all customers at the lowest interest cost: repo first, then term repo, MSF only for the last 20 crore.
games.lose: Going to MSF while repo room is left charges the penalty and shows RBI's 'careless bank' stamp; asking past 1% of NDTL under MSF is refused with the limit shown on the magnifier.
games.concept: MSF: overnight loan against SLR securities, up to 1% of NDTL

games.player_does: Splits a bank's NDTL into CRR (RBI vault), SLR (cash, gold or securities), loans and idle money, with customers arriving at random.
games.process_happens: An income meter runs: CRR earns 0, SLR securities earn some, loans earn most; idle money earns nothing until moved into G-secs.
games.win: Meet the CRR and SLR rules and keep idle money near zero by lending or buying G-secs.
games.lose: Keeping less than the CRR/SLR rule flashes a penalty; leaving money idle shows the income meter stalled.
games.concept: lendable money: lent vs idle, idle parked in G-secs

games.player_does: Given the repo rate line on a chart, sets the MSF line for each period by choosing the penalty (0.25%, 1%, 3%).
games.process_happens: The MSF line is drawn above repo and the gap bar appears with its value; trying to set MSF below repo is blocked.
games.win: MSF always above repo, and the chosen gaps match the periods the video shows.
games.lose: An MSF line at or below repo flashes the rule 'MSF = repo + penalty' and asks why a bank would ever use repo then.
games.concept: MSF rate = repo rate + penalty

games.player_does: Works an 'investment gate' desk: deal cards arrive (a foreign firm buys 12% of an Indian company, a pension fund buys 3% of shares on the exchange, a foreign phone maker builds a plant, a hedge fund buys 2%) and the learner sends each through the FDI gate or the FPI gate.
games.process_happens: The chosen route draws on the anchor picture: the elbow 'stake' arrow onto a company, the straight arrow to a new factory, or the arrow through the stock exchange; a stake bar on each card fills to its percent against a marked 10% line.
games.win: All deals routed correctly; the tree under 'invest' fills both branches.
games.lose: Sending a 3% buy to FDI shows its stake bar stopping below the 10% line and the deal bouncing back to the FPI gate.
games.concept: FDI vs FPI (10% line; stake or factory)

games.player_does: Runs a foreign phone company selling in India and chooses each year: keep shipping phones in, or build a factory in India.
games.process_happens: Shipped phones pass a customs gate that adds duty to each phone's price; factory phones skip the gate and use cheaper local labour, so their cost tag is lower; a policy card can add a government incentive.
games.win: Reach the lowest cost per phone, which happens only after choosing the factory (FDI route 2).
games.lose: Staying with shipping shows the duty stacked on every phone and a rival with a local factory undercutting the price.
games.concept: why companies choose FDI (customs duty, cheap labour, favourable policies)

games.player_does: Plays a foreign investor who wants Indian shares: chooses to register with SEBI as an FPI (picking the right risk category for its type) or to skip registration.
games.process_happens: A registered investor's money flows straight through the exchange to the company and shares come back; an unregistered one is stopped at the SEBI badge and can only hand money to a registered FPI, getting a P-note instead of shares.
games.win: Place three investor types (a central bank, a pension fund, a hedge fund) in categories I, II, III and get their money to the company by a legal route.
games.lose: Trying to go direct without registering lights the SEBI badge red and reroutes the money through the FPI with a P-note.
games.concept: SEBI registration, RFPI categories, P-note route

games.player_does: Orders cards: FIIs allowed (1994), QFIs allowed (2011), merger into FPI (2014), rename to RFPI, three risk categories.
games.process_happens: Each card grows the FPI tree: two panels appear, collapse into one band, the chip is relabelled, the three category branches drop down.
games.win: Tree complete in order.
games.lose: Placing the merger before 2011 shows nothing on the QFI side to merge, with a nudge to place QFI first.
games.concept: history of foreign portfolio investor categories

games.player_does: Holds the rupee on a rod under the moving dollar: picks a hard peg (rate locked at 5) or a crawling peg (±1% band) and responds as market pushes nudge the rupee up and down while gold drags the dollar along a rising line.
games.process_happens: The rate card shows the live rate; under a hard peg the rod is rigid, under a crawling peg the pin slides inside a yellow band.
games.win: Keep the rate inside the allowed band for ten ticks while the dollar moves.
games.lose: Letting the rupee drift outside the band snaps the rod and the rate card turns red, showing the peg has broken.
games.concept: pegging, hard vs crawling peg

games.player_does: Plays RBI at the dollar window under a fixed rate of 3.30: importers (the car buyer, a machine buyer, an oil buyer) queue with rupees asking for dollars, and RBI decides each round whether to pay out or devalue.
games.process_happens: Each payout lifts dollars off the forex reserve stack; a devaluation drops a new rate card (4.76, later 7.50) and every importer must now bring more rupees, so fewer can afford imports.
games.win: Finish ten rounds with reserves above zero and as few devaluations as possible.
games.lose: Paying out every request empties the stack and a 'balance of payment crisis' banner appears.
games.concept: how the fixed regime works and why central banks devalue

games.player_does: Links cards in order: dollar convertible into gold -> other currencies pegged to the dollar -> the system stands on this link -> US suspends convertibility -> Bretton Woods collapses -> India moves to a peg regime.
games.process_happens: Each correct link lights a segment of the 1944-1971 timeline; the final link drops the red cross at 1971.
games.win: Full chain lit with the cross at 1971.
games.lose: Putting the collapse before the suspension leaves the gold link standing, with a nudge that nothing has broken yet.
games.concept: why Bretton Woods collapsed

games.player_does: Places rate cards 3.30 (1948), 4.76 (1949), 7.50 (1966) and re-prices the 1-lakh-dollar car at each.
games.process_happens: The car's rupee tag updates (3.30 lakh, 4.76 lakh, 7.50 lakh) as each card is placed.
games.win: All three cards in order with the right car prices.
games.lose: A wrong car price shows the multiplication line with the wrong factor highlighted.
games.concept: India's devaluations and their effect on import prices

games.player_does: Works as the index office for one item, a chair: taps cities on a map of India to collect price quotes (base and current), drops each quote into the table, then chooses how to combine the price relatives (arithmetic or geometric mean).
games.process_happens: Each quote becomes a price relative (current / base x 100) in the column; the chosen mean produces the chair's elementary index; one outlier quote (a cheap base price that tripled) visibly drags the arithmetic mean up more than the geometric mean; the index then slides into the chair's row and is multiplied by its weight.
games.win: A correct elementary index from enough quotes, placed into the weighted total.
games.lose: Adding GST to a price shows the index jumping with a tax change ('fiscal policy moved WPI'); too few quotes shows a wide error band; the arithmetic mean shows the outlier's pull (answering the video's unanswered question).
games.concept: item index: quotations, price relative, geometric mean (Jevons)

games.player_does: Acts as policy maker watching three meters (PPI, WPI, CPI) on the supply chain; a random shock raises a producer's price, and the player decides when to pull a policy lever.
games.process_happens: The price pulse travels with a delay: producer band, then wholesale band, then consumer band; prices 10, 15, 20 tick up in turn; the lever slows the pulse only if pulled early.
games.win: Act on the PPI or WPI signal so CPI stays under the line.
games.lose: Waiting for CPI to move shows the rise already reaching shoppers; acting on no signal shows a needless slowdown.
games.concept: why a producer-side index warns early: a price rise travels down the chain

games.player_does: Sorts goods into the WPI basket groups: wheat, milk, raw cotton, jute, coal, electricity, sugar, noodles, chocolate, minerals.
games.process_happens: Each item drops into fuel and power, primary articles (food, non-food, minerals) or manufactured products (food products and others); a weight bar fills toward 13.15 / 22.62 / 64.23.
games.win: All items in the right group and sub-group.
games.lose: Putting sugar or noodles under food articles asks 'grown or processed?' and moves it to food products; putting raw cotton under food articles asks 'can it be eaten?'.
games.concept: food articles vs non-food articles vs food products

games.player_does: Sets the three group weights of a toy basket, then applies a 10% price shock to one group at a time.
games.process_happens: The index needle moves by weight x shock; a shock to manufactured products (heavy) moves it far more than one to fuel and power (light).
games.win: Predict which shock moves the index most before applying it, and get the real weights in the right order.
games.lose: A wrong guess shows the needle moving little or much with the weight-times-shock sum spelled out.
games.concept: WPI = sum of item index x weight / total weight (Laspeyres)

games.player_does: Fills a basket at today's shop and at the base-year shop, then turns the two totals into an index.
games.process_happens: Totals appear (1000 then, 5000 now), the price-relative formula turns them into 500, and the rise reads 400%; changing the base year changes every number.
games.win: Correctly state both the index (500) and the % rise (400%) from the same two totals.
games.lose: Saying the index is 400 shows the gap between 'index' and 'rise', with 100 as the base marker.
games.concept: basket and base year: comparing a fixed set of goods then vs now

games.player_does: As the government in the 1960s, watches a farmer and a small workshop owner get turned away by private banks, then chooses how many banks to nationalise (1, 6, 14) and when.
games.process_happens: Nationalised banks move into the yellow state zone; a share bar of banking business under the state fills (14 banks fill it to about 85%); the farmer and workshop now get loans, and village branches appear on a map.
games.win: Priority sectors receive credit and rural branches open across the map.
games.lose: Nationalising only one or two banks leaves the share bar low and the farmer still turned away, showing why the 1969 Act was on a mass scale.
games.concept: why mass nationalisation: private banks neglected agriculture and small industry

games.player_does: Places law sheets and committees on the timeline: SBI Act 1955, Subsidiary Banks Act 1959, Banking Nationalisation Act 1969, Acquisition Act 1980, CFS 1991, banking sector reforms committee 1998, LPG 1991.
games.process_happens: Each correct card changes the picture: the yellow zone grows, associate banks pop in, the era band forms, the band turns red, the committee row appears with I or II.
games.win: Full timeline built, ending with the 'part of' link from financial reforms into LPG.
games.lose: Putting the 1969 Act before the 'private banks neglect farms' problem card shows a law with no cause and asks for the problem first.
games.concept: 1969 and 1980 nationalisation Acts

games.player_does: Sorts policy cards (licence and permit control, government monopoly in key industries, banks nationalised, market-oriented approach, private participation encouraged) to either side of the 1991 line.
games.process_happens: Left side fills with state-hand pictures, right side with open-market stalls; the timeline band colours follow.
games.win: All cards on the correct side of 1991.
games.lose: A card on the wrong side flashes and shows the era band it belongs to.
games.concept: government's role before vs after 1991

games.player_does: Drags transaction cards (oil import, software export, NRI sends money home, foreign tourist stays in Goa, FDI in a factory, loan from World Bank, interest paid on that loan) onto the leaves of the BoP tree.
games.process_happens: Each correct card drops into its leaf's debit or credit board and that board's plus/minus updates; the account totals and the vault level move.
games.win: All cards placed; the tree's totals and the vault match the statement.
games.lose: Putting loan interest under capital-account loans bounces the card back with the principal-vs-interest rule shown on the two leaves.
games.concept: current account: visibles (BoT) and invisibles

games.player_does: As RBI for one year, approves or delays monthly dealings (big oil import, IT export contract, FPI pulling money out, foreign loan) while watching the forex vault.
games.process_happens: Dollar bundles flow along the globe-India loop; the vault's lockers fill or empty; at year end the four boards, two account totals and the BoP plus/minus are drawn.
games.win: Finish the year with the vault never empty.
games.lose: If a negative BoP is larger than the vault, the lockers empty and the screen names it a BoP crisis.
games.concept: BoP and forex reserve; BoP crisis

games.player_does: Given four head results (visibles -, invisibles +, investments +, loans -) with small amounts, works out the current balance, the capital balance and the BoP.
games.process_happens: Frames close around the heads as each total is entered; CAS or CAD label lights; the BoP arrow goes green into the vault or red out of it.
games.win: Correct signs and totals at all three levels.
games.lose: A wrong current-account sign makes the CAS/CAD label light wrongly and shows which heads were added.
games.concept: account balances, CAS/CAD and overall BoP

games.player_does: Plays an agency house between the Company and local merchants. The Company keeps demanding more goods; merchants say they lack money; the player decides how much to lend and at what interest, then opens a deposit window for the public and sets the deposit rate.
games.process_happens: Goods flow up the chain as loans flow down; public coins flow into the agency house; interest coins flow back from merchants and out to depositors; a profit meter shows the gap between the two rates. When deposits and loans both run, the player's square is relabelled BANK.
games.win: Meet the Company's demand without running out of funds, with deposit rate below loan rate, until the BANK label appears.
games.lose: Paying depositors more than borrowers pay drains the profit meter; refusing deposits leaves funds empty and the Company names a new agency house.
games.concept: public deposits at lower interest than loans: agency houses start working like banks

games.player_does: Gets crisis cards (trade obstacles in Indian markets, merchants short of cash, agency houses' big profits, World War I panic, Great Depression) and response cards (agency houses, short-term loans, presidency banks, Imperial Bank merger, RBI Act and RBI) and links each crisis to its response on a growing timeline.
games.process_happens: Each correct link plays its scene on the line (a wall and a middleman strip, a loan arrow, three banks rising, three buildings sliding into one, a law sheet arcing to the RBI coin).
games.win: All pairs linked and placed in the right order of years.
games.lose: Placing the RBI before the Depression shows an empty crisis slot: 'no crisis yet that demanded it'.
games.concept: Great Depression, RBI Act 1934 and the RBI (1935) with its powers

games.player_does: During a war-time panic, depositors queue to withdraw from three separate small banks; the player can merge banks into one before the queue reaches them.
games.process_happens: Each bank's reserve bar drains as people withdraw; an unmerged small bank empties and its building cracks; merged banks pool assets and survive longer.
games.win: Keep the merged bank open through the panic and name two benefits of merging.
games.lose: A bank left alone fails and the failure spreads panic to the next queue.
games.concept: World War I panic, bank failures and the 1921 Imperial Bank merger

games.player_does: Sets next January's price index each year by choosing how many points to add.
games.process_happens: A bar for last year's index (the divisor) grows under a smaller bar for the rise; the inflation % is worked out live and written under the year, the way the video's table does.
games.win: Meet missions such as 'keep inflation at exactly 10% for three years' (needs a bigger rise every year) or 'make inflation fall while the index still rises'.
games.lose: Adding a flat 10 points each year when 10% inflation was asked gives 10%, 9%, 8.3%, and the screen labels it: same rise, bigger base, smaller %.
games.concept: base effect

games.player_does: Drags 'base year' and 'previous year' tags onto the Price Index row and the Inflation % row, then picks which cell is the divisor for each year's inflation.
games.process_happens: A correct pick draws the arc from the right cell, as in the video; a wrong pick computes the % against the base year and shows a much larger number.
games.win: All tags and divisors placed correctly.
games.lose: Using the base year as divisor gives 30% for 2015 instead of 8.3%, showing why the reference year matters.
games.concept: index vs inflation reference year

games.player_does: Plays the borrower at a 1970s bank counter: asks for a lower rate, raises the loan amount, or points to the rival bank's offer.
games.process_happens: The clerk's rate tag is struck and rewritten lower with each move, keeping the ladder visible; then three other borrowers of the same bank appear with their own bargained rates.
games.win: Get a low rate, then see the side-by-side tags and correctly light the two missing chips: no transparency, no standardisation.
games.lose: Accepting the first offer leaves the learner at 15% while a neighbour pays 3% for the same loan, which is exactly the PLR problem.
games.concept: bargained rates under PLR and why they lacked transparency and standardisation

games.player_does: Plays RBI: picks the rule (PLR: banks free; BPLR: rate for the best customer taken as the minimum; base rate: each bank's cost-based floor, below which lending is barred) and runs a year of lending by four competing banks.
games.process_happens: 100 loan tokens fall from the four banks onto a floor line; under BPLR competition pushes most of them below the line (about 77 of 100), under base rate none can cross it; the transparency and standardisation chips get a cross or a tick.
games.win: End a year with no loans below the floor and both chips ticked (only the base-rate rule does this).
games.lose: Choosing BPLR shows the tokens sliding under the floor and the banks' speech bubble 'minimum was your assumption'.
games.concept: why BPLR failed and the base rate held

games.player_does: Builds a bank's base rate by stacking blocks: cost of funds, operating expenses, minimum return, cost of keeping CRR (mechanic: build a rate from its parts).
games.process_happens: The stack's height becomes that bank's floor line; a second bank with higher operating expenses builds a taller stack; customers' requested rates below the line are refused.
games.win: Set two banks' floors correctly and explain why they differ.
games.lose: Leaving out operating expenses makes the floor too low and the bank lends at a loss, shown as a red cost bar sticking out above the rate.
games.concept: base rate calculation and why base rates differ by bank

games.player_does: Places cards on the era strip: bargained PLR (1973), BPLR (2003), 2010 report with 77% below BPLR, base rate (2010), new trouble and MCLR (2015).
games.process_happens: Each card drops a heading from its tick with the dotted line, as in the video, and the goal chips change from crossed to ticked at the base rate.
games.win: Strip complete with each system's failure leading to the next.
games.lose: Placing base rate before the 2010 report shows no reason yet for a new system and nudges the learner to place the evidence first.
games.concept: sequence of lending-rate systems

games.player_does: Runs a bank for several rounds: takes deposits, lends to borrowers of different risk, invests surplus, and chooses how much to keep aside as a cushion (the 'inner pocket').
games.process_happens: Each round a shock may hit: a borrower defaults (the interest loop gets a red cross), share prices drop, or a cyber attack hits; losses come out of the cushion first.
games.win: Survive all rounds with every depositor repaid while still earning interest.
games.lose: A shock larger than the cushion stamps the FAIL seal; depositors queue at other banks too (contagion), showing why Basel asks for money kept aside.
games.concept: Basel norms: keep money aside against risk

games.player_does: Sorts bank events into credit, market or operational risk: borrower does not repay, bond prices fall, server crashes, robbery, gold price swings, fraud by staff.
games.process_happens: Each correct card lights its entry on the sidebar risk map and plays its picture (crossed loop, falling price line, broken server).
games.win: All events placed correctly.
games.lose: A wrong card lights the wrong sidebar box and shows the event's real picture with its risk name.
games.concept: credit risk

games.player_does: Links the chain of a bank failure in order: bank fails, depositors lose savings, trust falls, runs on other banks, banks cannot lend, industry stops growing, economic downturn, world effect.
games.process_happens: Each correct link lights the next node and spreads a red tint from the first bank to others, then to factories and to a globe.
games.win: Full chain built from one bank to the world economy.
games.lose: A link out of order breaks the chain and shows the missing step (for example runs on other banks before trust falls).
games.concept: bank failure and its chain of effects

games.player_does: Holds a 10-year, 5%, 10,000 face-value bond that pays a fixed 500 a year. News cards arrive (recession, share market boom, better deposit rates); the player decides to buy or sell the bond and at what price in the secondary market.
games.process_happens: Demand meter moves with the news, buyers bid, the certificate moves to the new owner box, the 500 tag rides along, and the yield = 500 / price is computed and dropped as a dot on the yield-price graph.
games.win: Predict the direction of price and yield after each news card and end with the highest income on money paid.
games.lose: Buying at 15,000 in a panic shows the dot landing low on the curve (3.3%) and the rule 'paid more, same 500, lower yield'.
games.concept: bond yield: fixed 500 coupon, resale at 9K, 15K and a cheaper price gives 5.5%, 3.3%, 10%

games.player_does: Gets bond cards (face value, price paid, coupon) and drops each through the yes/no gate 'sold at a discount?' into zero-coupon or coupon bond.
games.process_happens: A timeline runs for each card: the zero-coupon bond pays nothing until maturity and then face value; the coupon bond drops its interest every year and the principal at the end; total return counters fill.
games.win: All cards sorted and the player can say which pays 500 once and which pays 500 every year.
games.lose: A coupon bond put in the zero-coupon bin shows its yearly interest coins falling out with nowhere to go, and the gate rule is shown.
games.concept: coupon rate: why anyone buys a bond without a discount; zero-coupon return

games.player_does: Plays the government needing money: drags security certificates to RBI, which sells them to banks and NBFCs in the primary market; then one bank sells its bond on in the secondary market.
games.process_happens: Money flows up to the government as certificates flow down; in the primary market the price is fixed by the government, in the secondary market a demand-supply slider sets it.
games.win: Raise the target amount and correctly say who sets the price in each market.
games.lose: Trying to set the secondary-market price as the government is refused with 'here buyers and sellers decide'.
games.concept: primary vs secondary market; secondary price set by demand and supply

games.player_does: As investor A holding an XYZ bond, each period chooses whether to buy CDS protection from seller B (paying a premium coin) or stay unprotected.
games.process_happens: Buying slides the RISK disc from A to B and the sleep inset turns to Z's; each period a premium coin flows from A to B; at random XYZ may default, which either triggers a payout from B to A (covered) or breaks A's bond (uncovered).
games.win: Finish the bond term with the money safe, a good sleep score and the least premium spent.
games.lose: A default while uncovered breaks the bond and A loses the principal (why protection exists); insuring a very safe bond for every period lets premiums eat the return (protection has a price).
games.concept: CDS risk transfer and premium

games.player_does: Switch roles and play seller B: decide how many CDS contracts to sell against B's cash buffer.
games.process_happens: Premiums from all buyers flow in each period; a default by XYZ makes B pay every buyer at once from the buffer.
games.win: Collect premiums and still have enough buffer to pay out if XYZ defaults.
games.lose: Selling too many contracts empties B's buffer on a default, showing that the risk did not vanish; it moved to the seller.
games.concept: risk transfer (who carries the risk after a CDS)

games.player_does: Arranges deals in a money market of five participants: drags a security from a borrower to a lender of choice (RBI, bank, NBFC, top-rated company, individual).
games.process_happens: Allowed deals animate the security down and cash up; the level ladder shows RBI at the top, banks and NBFCs in the middle, corporates and individuals below.
games.win: Complete a day's list of money needs using only allowed pairs (each deal within one level).
games.lose: Pairing an individual or a company with RBI bounces the deal and shows rule 2; trying to borrow without a security shows rule 1 ('no paper, no money').
games.concept: two rules: security first, then money; deal with your level or one level up or down

games.player_does: Plays ABC, a small supplier: ships goods to XYZ on two months' credit, sees production stall without cash, then chooses: wait, take a loan, or get XYZ to sign a bill of exchange and take it to the bank.
games.process_happens: With a signed bill, the bank discounts it: cash (90,000 against 1 lakh) rises to ABC at once, production restarts, and on the due date XYZ's payment drops to the bank, closing the loop.
games.win: Keep the factory running through the two months at the lowest cost.
games.lose: Going to the bank without XYZ's signature is refused; waiting stops production for two months; a loan costs interest and needs collateral.
games.concept: commercial bill: a bill of exchange discounted at a bank

games.player_does: Gets money-need cards and picks the instrument: government needs cash for 60 days, 182 days; a bank needs cash overnight; a bank needs cash for 25 days against its G-secs; a top-rated firm needs 50 lakh for 3 months; a bank raises 10 lakh for 6 months from the market.
games.process_happens: The chosen instrument's template fills (issuer, security down, cash up, limits); the checker tests issuer, tenure and minimum size.
games.win: Each need matched to an instrument whose issuer and limits fit (CMB, T-bill, call money, repo, CP, CD).
games.lose: A mismatch shows the broken limit: a company issuing a T-bill, a 3-lakh CP under the 5-lakh minimum, a CMB for 120 days.
games.concept: treasury bill: government security sold at a discount through RBI

games.player_does: Runs a bank short of cash for 25 days: chooses to sell securities outright to RBI or sign a repo, and sets the buy-back day.
games.process_happens: Repo: two securities go up to RBI inside a contract frame, cash comes down; on day 25 the cash goes back with interest and the securities return (the buy-back flow the video never drew); the same deal is relabelled reverse repo when viewed from RBI's chair.
games.win: Meet the cash need and get the securities back.
games.lose: An outright sale leaves the bank without its securities when it needs them again; missing the buy-back day breaks the agreement.
games.concept: repo: sell government securities to RBI with a buy-back agreement; reverse repo from RBI's side

games.player_does: Places loans of 1 day, 5 days, 14 days and 20 days on a time line, and ticks who may lend or borrow (banks, co-operative banks, IDBI, LIC, a mutual fund).
games.process_happens: Each loan falls into call money, notice money or term money; the permission table fills, and an insurer trying to borrow is stopped.
games.win: All loans in the right band and all permissions right.
games.lose: Putting a 5-day loan under call money shows the 1-day band; letting LIC borrow shows the red cross under 'borrow'.
games.concept: call, notice and term money: inter-bank lending for 1-14 days; who may lend and borrow

games.player_does: Starts a village co-op bank with 100 members who pool 1 lakh each. Keeps CRR and SLR as RBI requires, then sets the deposit rate, the loan rate and how much to lend to members who ask for loans, against a commercial bank offering 4% and 12%.
games.process_happens: The 100-lakh bar splits into CRR (to RBI at 0%), SLR (into bonds at 6%) and the lending slice; loans flow to the borrowers; at year end the tally fills: loan interest and bond interest in green, expenses and deposit interest in pink, and the profit (or loss) is shared as dividend.
games.win: Members are better off than with the commercial bank (deposit rate above 4%, loan rate below 12%) and the tally ends at zero or above.
games.lose: Paying 6% on deposits and lending at 8% turns the tally red; skipping CRR/SLR brings an RBI penalty notice.
games.concept: worked village example: 100 members, 1 crore, CRR/SLR, loans at 10%, deposits at 5%, profit 58,000

games.player_does: Builds a state's cooperative structure: drops PCS and UCB squares into district frames, places DCCBs and the state bank, then draws service arrows down the tree.
games.process_happens: Each correct placement lights its tier band; service arrows animate money support from the state bank to DCCBs to the societies below.
games.win: One DCCB per district, one state bank per state, every society connected to support.
games.lose: A second DCCB in the same district is refused with 'one per district'; an unlinked PCS shows 'no source of support'.
games.concept: district and state tiers (DCCB, state cooperative bank) and who serves whom

games.player_does: Matches each regulator (RCS, RBI, NABARD) to the bank types it covers, then counts regulators per type.
games.process_happens: YES marks fill the grid into a staircase; types with two regulators get a 'dual control' brace, three a 'triple control' brace, and a short reason pops for each link (licence, inspection, registration).
games.win: Grid correct and the dual and triple control labels placed on the right rows.
games.lose: Putting PCS under RBI shows 'no banking licence, so not under RBI'; putting UCBs under NABARD shows the all-India workload reason.
games.concept: RBI and NABARD roles; dual and triple regulatory control

games.player_does: Acts as a survey officer: for each spending group (food, pan and tobacco, housing, fuel and light, clothing and footwear, miscellaneous) chooses how many past days to ask a household about: 7, 30 or 365.
games.process_happens: A month of a sample family's spending plays as a calendar; with the chosen window the estimate of yearly spending is drawn beside the true value; a short window on clothing catches a month with no purchase (or a Diwali splurge) and badly misjudges the year.
games.win: Each group's estimate lands close to the truth (short window for frequent buys, long window for rare buys); the set is labelled MMRP.
games.lose: One window for all shows URP and its errors; two windows shows MRP; a 7-day window on housing gives zero rent.
games.concept: reference period: 7 days, 30 days or 365 days by how often a thing is bought

games.player_does: Drags about 30 household purchases (milk, bhujia, a cigarette pack, rent, a bulb, firewood, slippers, a fridge, a necklace, a car) into six group panels.
games.process_happens: Each panel fills; the group's weight bar grows for urban and rural baskets side by side (food large in rural, housing absent in rural).
games.win: All items in the right group.
games.lose: Putting rent under miscellaneous shows housing's own panel; putting a gas cylinder under food shows fuel and light.
games.concept: six groups of consumer spending

games.player_does: Matches four workers (clerk, factory worker, farm labourer, rural labourer) to their baskets and indices, then each index to its use (dearness allowance or minimum wage).
games.process_happens: A price rise in the basket moves the matched index, and the index flows down to the worker's pay: DA rises in the clerk's or government worker's salary; the minimum wage rises for farm and rural workers.
games.win: Every worker's pay keeps pace with the price rise in his own basket.
games.lose: Using the clerk's index for a farm labourer shows his basket (mostly food) rising faster than his wage: the reason segment indices exist.
games.concept: uses of segment CPIs: dearness allowance and minimum wage

games.player_does: Prices one item, an egg: collects 10 market quotes (base and current), turns each into a price relative, takes the mean, then places the egg's index into the urban basket with its weight; repeats for one more item and a group.
games.process_happens: Price relatives fill the column, the geometric mean gives the egg's index; the index times its weight joins the weighted sum; the food group's index then joins the six-group sum and CPI-Urban appears.
games.win: CPI-Urban computed with every item weighted correctly.
games.lose: Forgetting the weight shows the egg (weight 0.36) moving CPI as much as cereals (6.59); an arithmetic mean shows how one quote that doubled pulls the item index up more.
games.concept: CPI-Urban = sum of item index x weight / total weight (Laspeyres)

games.player_does: Splits 100 points of weight across the six groups for an urban family and a rural family from short descriptions of their spending.
games.process_happens: The player's columns are laid beside the official ones; a food price shock is applied and both CPIs move by weight x shock.
games.win: Food highest in both, rural food above half, rural housing near zero; predict which CPI rises more after a food shock.
games.lose: Giving rural housing a big weight shows rent as negligible in villages; underweighting food shows the rural index missing a food-price rise.
games.concept: group weights in the urban, rural and combined baskets

games.player_does: Splits a bank's NDTL of 2000 crore: drags money into the CRR vault at RBI, into the SLR safe (choosing cash, gold or G-secs), and into the lending pool, under rules set by RBI (for example CRR 4.5%, SLR 18%).
games.process_happens: An income meter runs: the vault earns 0, the safe earns a little, loans earn most; then a bank-run event sends a queue of depositors to the counter and the safe's liquid assets are sold to pay them.
games.win: Meet both ratios, survive the bank run and end with the highest income.
games.lose: Keeping less than the rule triggers the fortnightly report's penalty loop; too little in the safe makes the bank fail the run.
games.concept: SLR: share of NDTL kept by the bank in gold, cash or G-secs as a bank-run cushion

games.player_does: Plays RBI with CRR and SLR dials facing a scenario card (prices rising fast, or a slowdown).
games.process_happens: The lendable share of NDTL recomputes (100 - CRR - SLR), the rain of loan arrows to the borrower crowd thickens or thins, and a demand and inflation meter follows.
games.win: Bring inflation or growth into the target band with the right direction of change.
games.lose: Cutting the ratios while prices are already rising pushes the inflation meter into the red, with the chain 'more loans, more purchasing power, more demand'.
games.concept: raising or cutting CRR/SLR to control inflation or support growth

games.player_does: Places rule cards (CRR 3-15%, CRR up to 15%, interest on CRR 1999-2007, SLR 25-40%, SLR up to 40%) into the era table and moves the committee figure to the right turning point on the CRR and SLR curves.
games.process_happens: Each correct card fills its cell; placing the committee at 1991 makes the curves bend down and the SLR circle slide from 38.5% to 25% at 1997.
games.win: All rules in the right era and the committee at the right turning point.
games.lose: Putting the floor removal before 2007 shows the law icon refusing ('the amendment came in 2007').
games.concept: 1991 committee and the fall of SLR from 38.5% to 25% by 1997

games.player_does: Works a 'data desk': picks the latest report from a list drawn by BIE, reads its as-on date, finds Total Reserves in US$ million, converts it to billion, then divides by a given monthly import bill.
games.process_happens: Each right pick zooms and highlights the way the video does; an import-cover meter fills in months as the last step is done.
games.win: Correct total in billions and the right months of import cover.
games.lose: Reading a variation column gives a small (even negative) number and the screen says 'this is the change, not the stock'; reading the publish date as the data date flags the one-week lag.
games.concept: reading the RBI forex report (as-on date, total, import cover)

games.player_does: Fills an empty vault with the four parts (foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs, reserve tranche), choosing how big each block is.
games.process_happens: Blocks stack into the vault and a total counter rises; the real shares from the report are revealed beside the player's guess.
games.win: Total matches and the largest part is placed correctly.
games.lose: Making gold or SDRs the biggest block shows the real break-up, where foreign currency assets are by far the largest.
games.concept: component break-up of forex reserves

games.player_does: With a limited budget, places bank types over the 140-crore crowd: a costly commercial branch, a cheap small bank locked to one licensed district, or a payments bank reaching people through phones.
games.process_happens: The yellow 'reached' shade grows over the crowd where each bank serves; clusters of farmers, small shops and city-slum households light up when reached.
games.win: Shade at least the target share, including the marginalised clusters and an urban slum cluster, within budget.
games.lose: Spending everything on commercial branches reaches few people; placing a small bank outside its licensed district gets an RBI 'not allowed' stamp.
games.concept: financial inclusion and the roles of small and payments banks

games.player_does: Drags service cards (accept deposits, payments, remittance, internet banking, give loans, open an NBFC) into the licence of a small bank or a payments bank.
games.process_happens: Allowed services settle into the bank's list; 'give loans' dropped on the payments bank is struck in red with the credit-risk reason, and 'open an NBFC' draws a dotted arrow that hits a red X.
games.win: Both licences filled correctly.
games.lose: A wrong placement plays the struck line or the blocked arrow and asks why (no credit history, high defaults).
games.concept: what a payments bank may and may not do

games.player_does: Plays a wallet company growing from bill payments to a payments bank: applies to RBI, picks a name, picks services, and tries a shortcut to lending.
games.process_happens: The wallet icon passes the RBI licence card if criteria are met; a name without 'Payments Bank' is sent back; the lending shortcut through an NBFC is blocked.
games.win: Becomes a licensed payments bank serving people who never had an account.
games.lose: Trying to lend or to skip the name rule shows RBI's reason and resets that step.
games.concept: how and why payments banks were created and limited

games.player_does: Links each reason traditional banks fail (high running cost, high fees, unsuitable products) to the small-bank feature that answers it (tech-driven, targeted, flexible).
games.process_happens: Each correct link draws a line from the pink reason box to the lit sidebar feature and shades a little more of the crowd.
games.win: All three reasons answered and the crowd shade grows.
games.lose: A wrong link shows the reason box staying pink and the crowd unchanged.
games.concept: why differentiated banks were designed this way

games.player_does: Runs a small country year by year with two sliders: GDP growth and population growth.
games.process_happens: Two lines draw: GDP and per capita income; a stretch is labelled PERIOD OF ECONOMIC GROWTH only while per capita income keeps rising.
games.win: Produce five years of sustained per capita growth.
games.lose: Raising GDP while population grows faster makes per capita income fall; the growth title turns pink and gets a red cross, as in the video.
games.concept: growth = sustained rise in per capita income

games.player_does: As the government, splits each year's extra national income among healthcare, education and defence.
games.process_happens: The crowd's below-poverty-line and literacy meters respond; the benefit arrow from the growth card reaches the crowd only when health and education get enough.
games.win: Growth years that also show poverty falling and literacy rising: the staircase figure steps up to DEVELOPMENT.
games.lose: Putting it all into defence keeps growth on but crosses the benefit arrow and worsens the meters, showing growth without development.
games.concept: growth vs development (quality of life)

games.player_does: Orders cards: terms used as one before 1960, trickle-down theory popular, 1960s data of high growth with low quality of life, theory fails, 1970s distinction, the open question of measuring development.
games.process_happens: Each placed card adds its piece to the timeline picture (note, theory line, crossed arrow, staircase, empty tape).
games.win: Timeline complete with the empty measuring tape at the end.
games.lose: Putting the 1970s distinction before the failure shows nothing yet to disprove, with a nudge to place the evidence first.
games.concept: history of the growth-development distinction

games.player_does: As the government in the 1950s, chooses how to bring banking to regions on a map of India: build new government banks (cost and years) or take over existing ones (Imperial Bank with 450+ branches, princely-state banks).
games.process_happens: Branch pins light up on the map; a year counter and a budget meter run; taken-over banks move into the yellow 'nationalised' zone on the timeline and get the emblem.
games.win: Banking reaches most regions within a few years and budget.
games.lose: Building only new banks drains the budget and leaves villages dark for years, showing why the quicker route was chosen.
games.concept: why independent India needed nationalised banks

games.player_does: Places RBI and SBI events: RBI Act 1934, RBI opens in Calcutta 1935, head office to Bombay 1937, independence 1947, Transfer to Public Ownership Act 1948, RBI nationalised 1949, SBI Act 1955, Associates Act 1959.
games.process_happens: Each correct card animates its picture: dotted hop to Bombay, law sheets dropping, emblem raised over RBI, Imperial name struck and SBI written, associates panel.
games.win: Timeline complete with the nationalised zone spanning 1949-1959.
games.lose: Placing the 1949 nationalisation before the 1948 Act shows an institution change with no law behind it and asks for the law first.
games.concept: RBI from private to public: Act clause, 1937 move, 1948 Act, 1949 nationalisation

games.player_does: Drags each associate bank to its princely-state region on a map.
games.process_happens: Each matched bank gets a State chip and an SBI link line; when Jaipur and Bikaner are both placed a MERGED frame closes round them; a 92% share bar shows partial ownership.
games.win: All eight placed, SBI's reach drawn across the regions, seven banks after the merger.
games.lose: A wrong region shows the bank's real home state lit and the region left without SBI presence.
games.concept: SBI associate banks (1959) and partial nationalisation

games.player_does: Gets a 'statement court' built from one chapter: 3-4 statements, each true or with exactly one changed element (a number 41% to 45%, a category non-tax to liability, an extreme word like 'single-handedly'). For each, the player drags it onto the lesson node that decides it and rules true or false.
games.process_happens: The chosen node opens as a short replay of the lesson scene (the receipts tree, the devolution fork); the changed element in a false statement lights up against the node's real value, and the options grid crosses every option that contains a false statement.
games.win: Correct verdict on each statement with the right evidence node; the surviving option is the answer.
games.lose: Ruling a false statement true shows the node with the conflicting value side by side (41% vs 45%) and leaves wrong options standing; picking the wrong node shows 'this node does not decide this statement'.
games.concept: statement elimination: one false statement removes every option that contains it

games.player_does: Elimination race (new mechanic): faces a multi-statement question with an options grid and a check budget; chooses which statement to check first, each check costs one coin.
games.process_happens: Each check reveals true or false, and the grid crosses every option the verdict rules out; a counter shows how many options each check removed.
games.win: Reach a single surviving option in the fewest checks (for Q6, checking statement II alone leaves only (c)), then make one confirming check.
games.lose: A check that removes no option is shown as 'wasted'; running out of coins with two options left forces a guess and shows which check would have split them.
games.concept: statement elimination: one false statement removes every option that contains it

games.player_does: Runs a budget: drags the question's figures (revenue receipts, revenue expenditure, capital spending, borrowing, interest, non-debt receipts) into a picture of a receipts bar, an expenditure bar and the gap.
games.process_happens: The gap block grows or shrinks; it is named fiscal deficit and must be filled by borrowing; the revenue box shows its own shortfall (revenue deficit); removing the interest slice from the gap leaves the primary deficit. Live numbers update on each block.
games.win: All figures in the right slots; the three deficits shown match a statement set or an option.
games.lose: Each wrong slot produces one of the exam's trap answers and says which mistake made it (adding interest gives 51,500; subtracting non-debt receipts again gives 58,500 in Q5).
games.concept: primary deficit = fiscal deficit - interest payments (Q4 statement III, then Q5)

games.player_does: Sorts government money items into capital or revenue receipts and, within revenue, tax or non-tax: borrowings, disinvestment, loan recovery, interest received on loans, PSU dividends, GST.
games.process_happens: Each item flows to the government emblem; a liability meter rises only when borrowing comes in (with a return arrow for principal plus interest); an asset meter falls on disinvestment.
games.win: All items sorted, with the liability and asset meters explaining each capital receipt.
games.lose: Putting interest received under capital receipts shows the liability meter refusing to move: no one has to be repaid.
games.concept: interest received on loans is non-tax revenue, not a liability (Q1 statement III)

games.player_does: Acts as the Finance Commission: first sets the vertical share of the divisible tax pool for states, then splits the states' share across criteria weights.
games.process_happens: The pool splits centre vs states; a stacked bar of criteria fills slice by slice; sample states receive more or less as weights move (income distance favours poorer states, tax effort rewards collection).
games.win: Match the commission's recommended split and explain who gains from one criterion.
games.lose: Entering 45% shows the recommended 41% next to it; a criteria set that does not add up to 100% will not lock.
games.concept: 15th Finance Commission: 41% vertical devolution, weighted horizontal criteria incl. tax effort (Q6)

My income, then my family's, then the country's: a sum the learner already knows how to do grows into national income.
A one-laptop economy makes the three-way equality checkable with four small numbers.
The same 10,000 lands on spending, products and income one after another, which proves the claim on the picture itself.
A dot climbing the curve while both axis bars change makes the trade-off a movement the learner watches, not a sentence.
The critique is shown on the same curve: 'Short Term' is struck, 'long term' is written, and the dot slides back.
Push arrows squeeze a dot that will not move while hatch lines pile up: NAIRU is seen before it is named.
Telling the topic as an idea that was believed and then challenged gives the lesson a story arc and a reason to listen.
'Schedule' is unpacked to the plain word suchi / list, which makes the whole term obvious.
Voices the learner's doubt (what difference does it make?) before giving three concrete benefits.
Names a common wrong belief (unscheduled = unregulated) and corrects it with the licence rule.
The root-cause hunt asks 'what does this depend on?' link by link, so the learner discovers what monetary policy must control before it is named.
The rich house owner who cannot buy a 25 lakh plane makes 'blocked money' unforgettable, and the voiced objection (sell the house) defines liquid money for free.
The CONTROL arms move to liquid money and the chain folds into the MONETARY POLICY badge exactly as the term is said.
'Let us break down this whole statement': the official one-line definition is unpacked phrase by phrase, each phrase becoming one step of the work.
A basket of mixed banknotes tied to the rupee note by a rope makes 'pegged to a basket' literal.
The weighted average is built in a table with assumed weights and real-looking rates, so the NEER is computed, not just defined.
'Think with a cool head' and 'I am sure you can work out the purpose yourself' make the learner infer before the answer.
Justifies the order of the next lessons (floating before LERMS) by prerequisite, not by date.
The rule is built first, so stagflation lands as a surprise twist: one red row breaking two green ones.
The word is split into STAG and FLATION, each half tied to its meaning: an easy memory hook.
The oil shock runs on the same resources -> economy -> GDP flow used at the start, so the cause sits where the learner already looks.
Running the scenario in reverse fills the second table row without a new explanation.
Analogy bridge: the known inflation question and its two indexes sit above the new currency question, so the learner expects two indexes before they are named.
The cause chain (many partners, many rates, cannot track each, need one index) gives the reason for the index before its method.
REER is taught as 'one small change' to the NEER table, so the second method costs only one new idea.
The 'but why?' question turns a claim into four reasons, and the 1-4 tab row keeps the learner oriented.
Everyday boasting stories and the newcomer's inner voice make market sentiment human.
After building the link, the contrast (short-term disconnect) stops the learner over-generalising.
The bond's cash-flow loop at a glance: investor's money up to the company, face value and coupon back on dotted arrows, both tagged fixed.
Fear then reassurance: the company runs away with your money, 'would you still invest?', then the spotlight of the rating agency on the issuer.
One bond passed along a chain of investors with the coupon arrow redrawn to the current holder: 'the coupon follows the bond' as a picture.
A column of return under each holder: the first reads coupon rate, the later ones 'more or less', then they are boxed and renamed bond yield.
The same chain is reused for primary and secondary market; only a coloured panel and the sidebar box move.
Seed in, harvest out: gross vs net with 10 and 100 before any formal word.
A machine's value curve falling to zero makes depreciation visible as a loss over time.
The formula is drawn as an arc from gross to net labelled '- depreciation' after two worked examples, so it reads as a summary, not a rule to memorise.
Two identical phones with YES and NO paths teach the boundary rule with one everyday object.
Starts from the learner's own loan and lifts it one level ('isi tarah banks bhi RBI se...'), so RBI's role is understood through a known act.
The policy effect is taught as a what-if with both directions on the same diagram (labels flip from decreased to increased), and LAF is named only after the effect is understood.
An explicit two-layer design: 'as a layman you now know enough; for UPSC we go deeper', so the learner gets the big idea before the mechanism.
The name 'repo' is unpacked from the deal itself ('we call it a loan but it is a sale and a purchase', hence repurchase agreement).
The learner's objection (why borrow for only 24 hours?) is voiced and answered with a recalled concept (CRR/SLR).
Reverse repo is the repo picture mirrored, with arrows reversed and 'repurchase' changed to 'resell'.
One curve, three slopes, three terms: each term is a shape the eye can check, and the definitions are built from one another (rate lower, then rate negative).
The same colour code is found again on real CPI data, so the made-up curve turns into a reading skill.
The counter-intuitive question (falling prices, falling demand?) is voiced as the learner's own doubt and answered through buyers' expectations.
Reflation is named only after the harm chain, so the term arrives as the answer to a felt problem.
A claim the learner just accepted (factor cost rises only with production) is shown, then stamped with a red cross: inflation opens the lesson.
Quantity stays 1 in every row while the laptop's price climbs 10K, 11K, 12.1K: GDP rises with nothing more made.
